Storms and gales hit Poland: homes flooded, trees down and thousands of emergency callouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:36:38 UTC
18:36:38 KST

Night storms hit residents in many parts of Poland. Firefighters responded over 4,000 times; 12 scout camps were evacuated as a precaution amid floods and power cuts.
Across the country, firefighters are battling to deal with the weather front moving across Poland. Since midnight they have already responded to more than 4,000 call-outs to remove fallen trees, secure damaged roofs and pump water from flooded streets and buildings, the State Fire Service reported at 10:00 on Saturday.
Due to the forecast weather conditions, 12 scout camps have also been evacuated as a precaution. "Participants and staff have been taken to permanent buildings" - Brigadier Karol Kroć from the State Fire Service told the Polish Press Agency. He stressed that so far there have been no reports of injuries.
By midnight, eight camps had been evacuated: one each in Lower Silesia and Małopolska, two in Mazovia, two in Wielkopolska and two in Warmia and Masuria. After midnight a further four camps had to be evacuated in Łódź Voivodeship.
Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that, in view of the strong gales and the meteorological situation, the Territorial Defence Forces remain on heightened alert to support public administration and emergency services in dealing with the effects of dangerous weather phenomena.
Most flooding in Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship
According to the duty officer at the Provincial Fire Service Command in Toruń, in the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship firefighters were most often called out to pump water from basements, properties and streets. There were far fewer interventions involving fallen trees and branches.
In Łódź Voivodeship firefighters mainly dealt with the effects of strong winds - fallen trees and broken branches. There were also several instances of water being pumped out, but no roofs were torn off. "It wasn't tragic, but reports are still coming in" - said the duty officer at the Provincial Crisis Management Centre in Łódź.
The situation is also difficult because of power cuts. Around 19,400 households are without electricity. The largest numbers of customers without supply are in the Tomaszów Mazowiecki area - around 5,500, Zgierz - 4,400, and Piotrków Trybunalski - 3,200.
Storms and strong winds in Wielkopolska
In Wielkopolska, overnight storms and heavy rainfall mainly caused trees to be toppled and local flooding of properties and basements.
In Warmia and Masuria firefighters recorded more than 90 call-outs related to heavy rain and strong winds. Most interventions involved pumping water from flooded roads, properties and basements.
Łyna exceeds warning level
The overnight rainfall, which locally reached as much as 90 mm, also affected water levels. The Regional Water Management Authority (RZGW) in Białystok reported that at the Olsztyn-Kortowo gauge the level of the Łyna river exceeded the warning level of 160 cm by 5 cm.
In the Bartąg area, water overtopped the embankments and then spread over wasteland and into the so-called encircling ditch. Allotment gardens in Olsztyn were also flooded. According to the RZGW, the situation on the Łyna is now beginning to stabilise and the water level is gradually falling. Services continue to monitor the state of the river.
In Mazovia the highest number of interventions were recorded by firefighters in Warsaw and the districts of Piaseczno, Grójec, Pruszków and Wołomin. "Reports are still coming in" - said Brigadier Łukasz Darmofalski of the Mazovian fire service.
Call for caution
Because of the strong wind, Kampinos National Park has appealed to residents and tourists to exercise particular caution. "Avoid open spaces and places exposed to the wind. During strong gusts, do not stop under trees" - the statement reminded. Before setting off on the trails, people were also advised to check the latest forecasts and weather warnings.
Due to the weather, the gardens of the Wilanów Palace Museum and the Royal Łazienki Park in Warsaw, as well as Warsaw Zoo, have been closed until further notice.
On Saturday the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management issued warnings for storms in the southwest of the country and strong winds in the Podlaskie, Mazovian, Łódź and Warmian-Masurian Voivodeships. Strong gusts of wind are also still occurring in the Warmian-Masurian, Pomeranian, Świętokrzyskie and Lublin Voivodeships.

What do we know about the plane crash in Croatia?
Police said the wreckage, along with the bodies of two passengers, was found after a lengthy search.

"In addition, Canada is continuing to maintain its prolonged retaliation against the United States, including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services," he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump signed three proclamations on July 20 to impose additional 50-percent tariffs on certain goods from Canada in response to Canada's "discriminatory treatment of American products." ■

Pollard sets out plan for UK to win NATO manufacturing work
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:30:10 BST
18:30:10 KST

The Ministry of Defence is working through a series of NATO mechanisms to secure British industrial benefit from the alliance’s push to expand collective manufacturing capacity, Luke Pollard has told Parliament in a written answer.
The Minister of State for Defence was responding to James Cartlidge, the Conservative MP for South Suffolk, who asked what steps the department is taking to ensure UK defence manufacturers benefit from the new NATO commitment.
Mr Pollard said the department is “leveraging NATO mechanisms, including the Defence Production Action Plan, the NATO Defence Industrial Production Board, and the Innovation Scale-Up Package, to boost an aggregated demand, improve interoperability, strengthen supply chain resilience, and provide clearer long-term demand signals to industry.”
He said the Defence Industrial Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan reinforce that approach by supporting collaborative programmes with allies, listing deep precision strike, air defence, autonomous systems, munitions production, future combat air and anti-submarine warfare.
Those programmes, he said, help British firms “access new export and multinational procurement opportunities and take advantage of the shift to ‘always on production’.”
The phrase points at what has become the central problem of European rearmament, defence manufacturing has historically worked to intermittent orders, with production lines opened for a batch and then closed, an arrangement that keeps peacetime costs down but leaves no capacity to surge when demand rises. The war in Ukraine demonstrated how long it takes to reverse that, particularly in artillery ammunition, where output could not be raised quickly because plants had closed, tooling had been scrapped and specialist suppliers had left the sector.
Aggregated demand is the mechanism NATO is using to address it. If several allies commit to buying the same equipment on a predictable schedule, a manufacturer can justify investing in capacity that no single national order would support, and smaller states gain access to production they could not sustain alone.
The commercial question for British firms is whether they end up as prime contractors on those programmes or as suppliers into consortia led from elsewhere. European Union funding instruments for defence production have generally restricted or discounted participation by non-member states, and Britain’s access to them has been the subject of negotiation since 2024, which is part of why the answer emphasises NATO mechanisms rather than EU ones.
Mr Cartlidge served as Minister for Defence Procurement in the previous government and now shadows the defence brief.

Government still weighing decision on restricting proxy voters, Hong Kong official says
Proposed changes to law on buildings management meant to combat bid-rigging but limits to proxy votes could be too strict, home affairs director says
Hong Kong authorities have yet to decide whether to restrict proxy voters at homeowners’ meetings to relatives or other flat owners of the same estate under proposed law amendments meant to combat bid-rigging, the home affairs director has said, arguing such a move could be overly strict.
Director of Home Affairs Priscilla To Kit-lai said on Saturday that the proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance were aimed at enhancing the legitimacy of proxy votes amid concerns that voting results could be manipulated by a minority.
But she said the government had yet to decide whether proxy holders should be limited to the owners’ relatives or other owners in the same estate.
“For example, an elderly person living alone has a familiar friend in a different housing estate who helps the person – that’s acceptable now,” she said on a television programme.
“But it might not be possible if we add proposed restrictions. We need to see if society feels this is too strict.”
Issues of building management and owner governance came under intense scrutiny during an independent committee hearing looking into the cause of the devastating fire at Wang Fuk Court that killed 168 people last November, with testimonies alleging bid-rigging and proxy vote collection.
In a consultation document released earlier this month, authorities laid out five major directions for proposed amendments to the Building Management Ordinance, which regulates incorporated ownership in buildings.

U.S. Navy awards second CHAOS contract for cheap missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:26:24 UTC
18:26:24 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its Rusty Dagger cruise missile under the CHAOS program.
- The award follows a $70 million CHAOS contract the Navy gave CoAspire in July for its RAACM-ER maritime missile.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Zone 5 Technologies a $65 million contract to build a maritime strike variant of its AGM-188 Rusty Dagger cruise missile under a new program aimed at fielding low-cost precision weapons for the U.S. and its allies.
The award is an Other Transaction Agreement, a contracting mechanism the Pentagon uses to move faster than traditional acquisition rules allow. CMG Networks brokered the deal on behalf of the Naval Aviation Systems Consortium. Under the agreement, Zone 5 will design, build, test, and deliver a CHAOS-specific version of the Rusty Dagger for the Navy’s Coalition Heterogeneous Affordable Offensive Strike program, which is intended to field affordable, scalable precision strike weapons against land targets and moving maritime targets.
“Zone 5 is proud to partner with the Navy on CHAOS and deliver industry-best scalable maritime strike capabilities to the U.S. and our allies,” said Thomas Akers, CEO of Zone 5 Technologies.
Zone 5 is working on the effort with PAE Munitions and its Precision Strike Weapons program office, PMX-201, the company said. Zone 5 said it will draw on its experience fielding precision strike weapons across multiple service branches and international partners to provide a strike capability it described as credible, affordable, and scalable.
The award is the second CHAOS contract the Navy has issued for a low-cost maritime strike missile. In July, the Navy selected CoAspire for a $70 million agreement to develop a ground-launched maritime variant of its Rapidly Adaptable Affordable Cruise Missile-Extended Range, known as RAACM-ER, which has a claimed range of about 1,800 km (1,120 miles).
The Rusty Dagger, designated AGM-188A by the U.S. Air Force, originated as a low-cost cruise missile developed for the Air Force’s Extended Range Attack Munition program, which began in 2024 to address long-range strike requirements tied to Ukraine. The missile falls in the 200 kg (450 pound) weight class, including a roughly 45 kg (100 pound) warhead, and is powered by a single PBS Aerospace TJ80 turbojet engine. Its air-launched range is reported to exceed 930 km (500 nautical miles) at high subsonic speed. The missile is built within the size and weight envelope of a Mk 82 general-purpose bomb, allowing it to be carried by aircraft already equipped to drop that weapon.
The Rusty Dagger has already seen combat use. Zone 5 has said the missile is in production for Ukraine’s Air Force, and reporting on Russian territory has documented missile debris linked to Zone 5 through a recovered guidance antenna. The Air Force has separately selected Rusty Dagger for its Family of Affordable Mass Munitions program, which called for producing more than 1,000 units in its first year of production, according to Zone 5. The Air Force’s proposed fiscal 2027 budget outlined plans to buy nearly 28,000 Family of Affordable Mass Munitions rounds over five years. The Air Force Research Laboratory separately awarded Zone 5 a $12 million contract in June 2026 to develop manufacturing technology intended to scale Rusty Dagger production, with work centered in Miamisburg, Ohio.
Zone 5 Technologies, based in San Luis Obispo, California, was acquired by Norway’s Kongsberg and now operates as a Kongsberg company. The company describes itself as an aerospace engineering and production firm focused on modular, open-architecture counter-UAS interceptors and affordable ground- and air-launched effects. Founded in 2011, Zone 5 employs more than 500 engineers, technicians, and support staff, with manufacturing operations in California, Texas, and Ohio.

DRC gets 16,520 Ebola vaccine doses amid deadly outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

The Democratic Republic of Congo has received its first shipment of more than 16,000 doses of an Ebola vaccine as authorities race to contain an outbreak that has killed more than 2,500 people and is spreading rapidly across six provinces.
A batch of 16,520 doses of the Ervebo vaccine arrived in Kinshasa late Friday, Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said, with more than 50,000 additional doses expected by Monday.
“These doses would strengthen the government’s response to Ebola and contribute to the protection of populations, with the support of our partners,” Kamba told reporters at Kinshasa airport.
The World Health Organization said Thursday that 70,000 doses of Ervebo would be supplied to Congo from the global Ebola vaccine stockpile. Of those, 20,000 doses will be used in a Phase 3 clinical trial examining whether the vaccine can protect against the strain responsible for the current outbreak, while 50,000 will be administered to frontline and health workers.
The vaccine, developed by Merck and manufactured in Germany, is licensed and recommended for outbreaks caused by the Zaire strain of Ebola. The current outbreak, however, is being driven by the Bundibugyo strain, for which no vaccine or specific treatment has yet been approved.
Scientists do not yet know whether Ervebo provides protection against Bundibugyo. Early evidence, including animal studies, suggests it could offer some cross-protection, prompting WHO experts this month to recommend a large-scale human trial.
Kamba said Ervebo has been used extensively in previous Ebola outbreaks, including during the major epidemic that struck Congo and neighboring countries between 2018 and 2020.
“This vaccine has already been used several times, and in particular on a very large scale during the 2018-2020 outbreak,” he said.
The latest outbreak, Congo’s 17th, was officially declared May 15 but is believed to have been spreading for weeks before that. It has reached 56 health zones across Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo provinces, many of which face severe health care shortages, limited government presence and persistent insecurity involving armed groups.
The Health Ministry’s latest situation update puts the number of confirmed infections at 5,290, including more than 2,500 deaths.
The outbreak is showing no signs of slowing. Julien Harneis, the United Nations’ senior Ebola coordinator, warned Friday that the epidemic is “growing exponentially.”
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, also warned that communities affected by the outbreak are not receiving enough support to contain the virus.
The group said training for health workers and community leaders must be urgently expanded, particularly on detecting suspected cases, referring patients and preventing and controlling infections within communities.
The uncertainty surrounding the Bundibugyo strain has increased the urgency of developing targeted vaccines. Two candidates are already in clinical trials, one developed by U.S.-based Moderna using mRNA technology and another by the University of Oxford in Britain.
A separate vaccine known as rVSV Bundibugyo is also being developed by Singapore-based Hilleman Laboratories and has been described by WHO as the most promising candidate specifically targeting the strain.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids and can cause severe fever and other life-threatening symptoms. The disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past five decades.

In a post on X on Saturday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the US announcement was “an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty” against the United Nations’ member states.

No state can compel foreign banks, enterprises or airports to renounce commerce with Iran, he said.

Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:10:17 UTC
18:10:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Somali pirates hijack oil tanker off Yemen in latest attack
Somali pirates hijacked an oil products tanker off Yemen, a Somali maritime security official said, the latest in a resurgence of piracy that has seen six commercial vessels seized since April across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean.
Six armed pirates hijacked the Eritrean-flagged M.T. Sibu 1 on Thursday about 136 nautical miles (252 kilometers) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen, and took it toward Somalia’s Puntland coast, the official, who has knowledge of the incident, told The Associated Press on Friday.
He spoke on condition of anonymity as he was not allowed to discuss the matter publicly.
The Sibu 1, managed by the UAE-based Qatrat Alnada Almasi Ship Management, was sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department last year for allegedly belonging to an Iranian “shadow fleet” used to transport petroleum products seeking to evade U.S. sanctions.
The tanker had 20 crew members aboard: 16 Indians, one Syrian, one Sudanese, and one Iraqi. The nationality of one crew member was not immediately known. The vessel’s previous port of departure and intended destination remained unclear.
The hijacking came three days after pirates seized the Lutuf, a Cameroon-flagged general cargo vessel, off Somalia’s coast. The vessel had 10 crew aboard, including six Indians, a Turkish national, a Georgian national and two Serbian security guards, according to maritime tracking reports.
The Sibu 1 is the sixth commercial vessel hijacked by Somali pirates since April 21, when the Palau-flagged tanker Honor 25 was seized off Somalia. Pirates later seized the Sward on April 26, the Eureka on May 2, the Asana on July 17 and the Lutuf on Aug. 17.
The attacks have occurred increasingly far from Somalia’s coastline, including the hijacking of the Eureka while anchored off Yemen and the Asana about 65 nautical miles (120 kilometers) southwest of al-Mukalla.
The International Maritime Bureau recorded 38 piracy and armed robbery incidents worldwide during the first half of 2026, including five hijackings. Somali pirates accounted for 94% of crew members taken hostage during that period, the bureau said.
Puntland’s Security Ministry said Friday that its investigations indicated that forces beyond Puntland’s control were behind the renewed piracy, but did not identify any group or country. The claim could not be independently verified.
Puntland said it had deployed security forces along its coast and condemned airstrikes that it said struck fishing vessels and property near coastal communities where hijacked ships were being held. It called on the countries involved to explain strikes near Garacad on Aug. 18 and Aug. 20.
The ministry did not identify who carried out the strikes, and the allegations could not be independently confirmed.

Massive drone and missile barrage
The Ukrainian Air Force reported intercepting 182 Russian drones, three aviation missiles, and six loitering munitions early Saturday morning.

Despite the damage to the Rozdilna station in the Odesa region and the fatalities in Kyiv, Ukrzaliznytsia stated that overall railway operations and train schedules remained unaffected.
The attacks occur just days before Ukraine marks its 35th Independence Day on Aug. 24. The Security Service of Ukraine had previously urged citizens to remain vigilant regarding potential Russian strikes and provocations surrounding the anniversary.

The Estonian politician was the country’s first ever European commissioner, starting from 2004. He took up the economic and monetary affairs post under then-European Commission President José Manuel Barroso, and later served as vice-president and transport commissioner from 2010 to 2014.
Advertisement
An economist by training, Kallas started his career as president of the Bank of Estonia in 1991, where he was one of the principal architects of the country’s monetary reform. In 1994, he founded the liberal-democratic Reform Party and was elected to the Estonian parliament the following year, when he became foreign affairs minister.
Kallas was a key figure in the Baltic country’s European trajectory: After his appointment as foreign minister, he oversaw Estonia’s bid to join the EU. He was prime minister in 2002, when the country concluded negotiations to become a member and was invited to join NATO.
His daughter, Kaja Kallas, was Estonia’s youngest-ever serving prime minister, holding office from 2021 to 2024. She is now the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs for Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s second term.

TikTok agrees to pay $400 million to settle US children's privacy lawsuit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:08:58 UTC
18:08:58 KST

“This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents,” associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. said.
TikTok has agreed to pay $400 million after reaching a settlement with the US Justice Department (DOJ) over a lawsuit alleging the app failed to protect children's online privacy.
"Under the settlement, TikTok will pay $300 million immediately and an additional $100 million upon entry of an order vacating a prior consent decree entered against TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly," the DOJ said in a statement.
The department and the Federal Trade Commission sued TikTok in 2024, alleging that the app had collected children's personal data without parental permission.
The lawsuit said that even accounts created in a "Kids Mode" designed for users under 13 had collected email addresses and other personal information.
The case dates back to 2019, when the US filed a Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) lawsuit against Musical.ly, which TikTok's Chinese parent company ByteDance bought in 2017 and then merged into TikTok. The COPPA rule requires websites to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting any personal information from children younger than 13.
“This settlement is a major victory for American children and parents,” associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. said. “This resolution secures a substantial recovery while reinforcing the protections that families expect and deserve.”
The DOJ noted in its statement that TikTok had "undergone significant changes to its ownership, management, compliance functions, and privacy practices" since the 2024 suit was filed.
"The company has implemented extensive measures designed to strengthen safeguards for younger users, improve age-related controls, and enhance parental oversight," it said, adding that this had "strengthened protections for millions of American families."
Euronews has reached out to TikTok for comment.

Rhodope narrow-gauge railway: 100 years of magic on the rails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:05:26 UTC
18:05:26 KST

Saturday 22 August 2026 11:25
Saturday, 22 August 2026, 11:25
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Some trains carry passengers. Others carry stories, emotions and memories. The Rhodope narrow-gauge railway is one of them. For a century now, it has been running between Septemvri and Dobrinishte, crossing the Rila, Rhodope and Pirin mountains and turning every journey into an encounter with a different Bulgaria — beautiful, peaceful and seemingly untouched by time.
August 1 marked 100 years since the first train set off on the Septemvri–Velingrad section — the beginning of a journey that today is not merely a railway line, but a true legend. To mark the anniversary, Bulgarian State Railways (BDZ) is preparing to restore a narrow-gauge steam locomotive, which will once again pull special trains along the iconic route.
- St. George’s Day in Yakoruda – a romantic journey on the narrow-gauge railway
- Narrow-gauge train in the Rhodopes tops The Guardian’s 10 best scenic rail journeys in Europe
We spoke about the magic of the narrow-gauge railway, its history, and its future with Kristian Vaklinov, chairman of the Association “For the Narrow-Gauge Railway” — a man who has made the preservation of this unique railway his personal cause.
PHOTO Kristian Vaklinov
According to him, the reasons why the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway is so beloved go far beyond its stunning scenery.
“It is unique not only because it is the only remaining narrow-gauge railway in Bulgaria. It is unique because it connects people, lives and mountains. The beautiful scenery, tunnels, bridges and the railway itself turn the journey into an experience unlike any other in Bulgaria”, Kristian Vaklinov says
PHOTO bdz.bg
An engineering feat built by hand
The history of the narrow-gauge railway is a story of hard work, perseverance, and engineering daring. Construction began in 1921, and just five years later, the first 39 kilometres between Septemvri and Velingrad had been completed.
What remains remarkable to this day is that much of the route was built by hand, carved through the rocks of the Chepino Gorge, long before modern machinery made such projects easier.
“This is a true tribute to the people who built the railway. Some even devoted their lives to it without ever imagining that, a hundred years later, their work would continue to inspire so many people. The railway has 35 tunnels and over 1,000 metres of elevation gain, climbing to the highest railway station in the Balkans — Avramovo. The twists and turns of the route are another part of what attracts people from around the world, who come to admire what has been achieved. They come to see it with their own eyes, having read online that Bulgaria has this little train that has been winding its way through the mountains for 100 years”, the association’s chairman notes.
PHOTO bdz.bg
When slow speed becomes an advantage
In a world where we are all constantly rushing, the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway seems to offer the opposite — a chance to slow down.
Today, the train travels at an average speed of around 38 kilometres per hour — something that was once seen as a drawback but has now become one of its greatest attractions.
Instead of rushing toward your destination, you have time to look out the window, follow the winding rivers, count the tunnels, and admire the centuries-old forests and steep mountain slopes.
PHOTO bdz.bg
Tourists from around the world
In recent years, interest in the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway has been steadily growing. More and more tourists are choosing it as a unique way to explore the mountains.
What is particularly interesting is that an increasing number of passengers now come from different countries and continents specifically to experience the legendary little train.
According to Kristian Vaklinov, this is the clearest evidence that the narrow-gauge railway has long since evolved beyond its role as a simple means of transport and is gradually becoming one of Bulgaria’s most recognizable tourist attractions.
PHOTO bdz.bg
The steam locomotive – a long-awaited return
One of the most exciting developments surrounding the railway’s centenary is the upcoming restoration of the steam locomotive.
For many years, it was the hallmark of the special anniversary trains, and for many people, travelling behind it remains one of their most unforgettable experiences.
“A steam locomotive brings a different kind of emotion. For children, it is a true wonder, while for older people, it is a journey back to cherished memories. We are all eagerly looking forward to seeing it run on the rails again”, Vaklinov says.
PHOTO BGNES
The big dream
As the narrow-gauge railway celebrates its 100th anniversary, it is also looking to the future.
Kristian Vaklinov believes its enormous tourism potential is yet to be fully developed. His vision include more heritage trains, panoramic carriages, and themed tourist routes that would make the journey an even more memorable experience.
He is convinced that the railway deserves to be developed not merely as a means of transport, but as a national treasure and a symbol of Bulgaria’s natural beauty and engineering heritage.
PHOTO bdz.bg
A journey that stays in your heart
At the end of the conversation, Kristian Vaklinov extended an invitation to everyone who has yet to experience the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway:
“Get on this little train. It will not simply take you from one station to another; it will show you a different Bulgaria — one that we rarely get to see through a car window.”
And perhaps that is the great secret of the Rhodope narrow-gauge railway.
It does not impress with speed, luxurious carriages, or modern technology.
It impresses with soul.
For 100 years, this little train has tirelessly crossed the mountains, bringing people and generations together and proving that the most beautiful journeys are not always the fastest.
Sometimes, they are the journeys that make us slow down, look out the window, and remember that the beauty lies in the journey itself.
PHOTO bdz.bg
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

“There is facilitation for some ships carrying Iraqi oil in the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, without elaborating.

“The Strait of Hormuz has an impact on the entire world, not just Iraq,” he said.

The request was raised during Qalibaf’s talks with Iraqi officials amid concerns over the impact of restrictions in the strategic waterway on Iraqi oil exports.

Tõnis Saarts: Estonia not prepared for the epochal shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:03:00 UTC
18:03:00 KST

Tõnis Saarts: Estonia not prepared for the epochal shift
It increasingly seems that Estonia is becoming a victim of its own past success. There is too much nostalgia for the successful models of decades past and too little willingness to take risks or engage in open debate about the challenges of a new era, Tõnis Saarts finds.
At a time when Estonia is celebrating the 35th anniversary of the restoration of its independence, we must acknowledge that the world around us is very different from what it was in 1991 or even just a decade ago. Fundamental changes have taken place in recent years in geopolitics, the economy and technology alike.
In geopolitics, the era of soft security, dominated by various hybrid threats aimed at indirectly influencing societies and public attitudes, is giving way to the imperatives of hard security. The latter involve a direct military threat to border states such as Estonia.
In economics, neoliberalism — an ideology advocating a minimal state that Estonia enthusiastically embraced in the 1990s — has by now largely fallen out of fashion in Europe. In technology, there is already talk of a fourth, artificial intelligence-driven industrial revolution. Estonia's e-state success story largely belonged to the era of the third industrial revolution.
Of these three shifts, the change in security policy paradigms is probably the greatest challenge for Estonia. From 1991 onward, we adapted extremely well to the U.S.-led liberal world order, in which countries that belonged to the relevant clubs, such as NATO and the European Union, and adhered to the principles of liberal democracy seemed to have their security automatically guaranteed.
That world order is crumbling and in the worst case it could be replaced by geopolitics based on pragmatic deals and spheres of influence. Estonia's elite still lacks a clear strategy for how to operate in the face of such a possible development.
From now on, we can no longer afford the luxury of focusing primarily on soft security threats, in which Russia seeks to influence our society's attitudes and our economy largely through indirect means. The threat of a direct military invasion has increased.
Hard security, which requires direct investment in defense through purchases of drones, artillery and ammunition, is considerably more expensive than soft security. Well-funded intelligence and security services were capable of handling the latter effectively. Unfortunately, it is already apparent that the Estonian public is not particularly willing to foot the bill for hard security in the form of a higher tax burden.
This brings us to the second major epochal shift, in the economy. For the past several decades, one economic ideology has dominated in Estonia: neoliberalism, the belief that markets are always more efficient than the state, taxes should be low, government should be lean and people should generally fend for themselves rather than rely on the state.
It is now becoming increasingly clear, however, that it is difficult to reconcile low taxes with the need for sharply higher military spending without eventually sending the country into a debt spiral, while also keeping the public satisfied that the tax burden is being distributed fairly. Sooner or later, this will mean either a significant shift in our tax policy or severe cuts in government spending.
Economists are increasingly talking about a post-neoliberal era in which governments take a much larger role in strategically directing economic development, invest more heavily in education and human capital and show determination in supporting the defense industry and the energy transition. A focus on free markets is giving way to a softer form of state capitalism.
Several countries that Estonia has tended to look down on, such as Lithuania, Romania and Croatia, appear to have adapted much better to the post-neoliberal era and have been outpacing us in economic development in recent years. This, too, should prompt us to think seriously about whether our successful economic policy model, which worked well 20 to 30 years ago, can also help us meet the challenges of today's world.
Third, another major shift is looming on the technological front. For decades, Estonia was proud of its e-state. Unfortunately, all of that belonged to the era of the third industrial revolution when small countries and small-scale developers really could accomplish great things if they correctly identified where technology was headed.
We are now in the midst of the fourth industrial revolution, whose defining feature is artificial intelligence. Its development is in the hands of technology giants and major powers at the forefront of technological development. It is much harder for small countries and small languages to stand out in this new competitive environment.
Estonia's problem is that we were too good in the context of past eras: exemplary at ensuring our own security under the liberal world order, among Eastern Europe's most exemplary students of neoliberalism and among the most enthusiastic adopters of new technologies.
There is a term in history and economic history: first-mover advantage. Countries that are best at recognizing the challenges and demands of a particular era can achieve great success by acting quickly and intelligently. That was Estonia in the 1990s and 2000s.
The tragedy of successful first movers, however, is that over time, various attitudes, ways of doing things and institutions become entrenched around the myth of their success. By the time they finally realize that the world has fundamentally changed in the meantime, generating a new sense of momentum in society is extremely difficult.
Looking at developments in Estonian society, it increasingly seems that Estonia is becoming a victim of its own past success. There is too much nostalgia for the successful models of decades past and too little willingness to take risks or engage in open debate about the challenges of a new era. Isamaa Chair Urmas Reinsalu summed up the prevailing mood in society perfectly at the latest Opinion Festival: "No experiments." Unfortunately, the world around us will not wait. It is racing ahead at full speed.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Canada orders more RS4 weapon systems for ACSV fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:02:25 UTC
18:02:25 KST

- Kongsberg signed a NOK 1.1 billion, about $118 million, follow-on contract with GDLS-Canada to supply PROTECTOR RS4 weapon systems for Canada's ACSV fleet.
- The RS4 order builds on a roughly NOK 500 million contract from May 2020 and comes as Canada has ordered 190 additional ACSVs in 2026.
Kongsberg has signed a contract worth NOK 1.1 billion, about $118.4 million, to supply additional PROTECTOR RS4 Remote Weapon Systems to General Dynamics Land Systems-Canada for the Canadian Army’s Armoured Combat Support Vehicle program.
The Norwegian defense company said the deal is a follow-on order building on previous RS4 deliveries for the same program. Kongsberg first won a contract worth roughly NOK 500 million in May 2020 to supply PROTECTOR remote weapon stations for the ACSV fleet, according to prior reporting.
“This contract confirms our customer’s confidence in the PROTECTOR systems and further strengthens our long-term partnership with GDLS-Canada,” said Kjetil Reiten Myhra, Executive Vice President, Kongsberg and President of the Defence Systems division.
“We are proud that the RS4 continues to be selected as a key capability for the Canadian Armed Forces’ modern vehicle fleet.”
The RS4 is a remotely operated weapon station that lets a vehicle crew fire from inside the hull rather than exposing a gunner in an open turret. It can be equipped with machine guns, automatic grenade launchers, and, on some configurations, anti-tank guided missiles. The system uses a stabilized, four-axis mount and sensor package designed to let a crew engage targets accurately while the vehicle is moving. Kongsberg said the RS4 is already fielded with defense customers worldwide and can be integrated across a range of vehicle types.
The Armoured Combat Support Vehicle is a family of eight variants built on the LAV 6.0 chassis, including ambulance, command post, and mobile repair versions. The Canadian government approved the 360-vehicle, $2.52 billion program in 2019, and GDLS-Canada has produced the vehicles at its plant in London, Ontario. The Army accepted its first ACSV in December 2020, and the program reached Initial Operational Capability in January 2025 with the delivery of the Troop/Cargo, Ambulance, and Command Post variants. Full Operational Capability is planned for 2028.
Canada donated 39 Troop/Cargo Vehicle variants originally built for its own fleet to Ukraine, with GDLS-Canada replacing those vehicles under the existing contract. As of August 2024, the Army had received 34 of a planned 49 ambulance variants.
Not every ACSV in the fleet carries an RS4. A Canadian Army official told Canadian Army Today in a report published in December 2024 that the service had been able to buy only 178 of the weapon stations due to cost and availability, even though every vehicle in the fleet is built to accept one. Vehicles without an RS4 instead carry a pintle-mounted C6A1 machine gun. The Canadian Department of National Defence told Shephard Media in February 2026 that it expected final deliveries of the existing RWS order that summer.
Canada has also moved to expand the overall ACSV fleet. The Army ordered 190 additional ACSVs this year to replace aging support vehicles and support NATO operations, according to a July 2026 report. Kongsberg’s announcement did not specify how many additional RS4 units are covered under the new NOK 1.1 billion contract or say whether the order is tied to that fleet expansion.

Shipbuilding now two thirds of Scotland’s defence jobs
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:00:53 BST
18:00:53 KST

Shipbuilding and submarine work accounted for 7,900 of the 12,200 jobs supported by Ministry of Defence spending with industry in Scotland in 2024/25, according to official statistics published on Friday, a rise of nearly 18 per cent on the previous year.
The figure represents close to two thirds of the Scottish total, and the increase of 1,200 jobs from 6,700 accounts for the bulk of the 800 net rise in defence industry employment across Scotland over the same period.
Other construction supported 800 jobs, with weapons and ammunition at 200 and aircraft and spacecraft also at 200.
The National Armaments Director Group attributed the concentration to the two frigate programmes, stating that the Type 26 supports 2,000 jobs at BAE Systems’ Govan and Scotstoun yards on the Clyde, while the Type 31 accounts for 1,250 directly employed at Babcock’s Rosyth yard in Fife.
Those two programmes therefore account for around 3,250 of the 7,900, with the balance spread across submarine support at Faslane, supply chain work and the wider marine engineering base.
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “From investing in naval shipbuilding expertise on the Clyde and at Rosyth, to our nuclear deterrent and submarine support at Faslane, to our world-leading strengths in cyber, space, advanced radar and electronic warfare, we are supporting thousands of jobs and opening exciting career pathways for young Scots.”
The department also points to Norway’s £10 billion Type 26 order, which it says will sustain over 2,000 jobs and support more than 100 Scottish businesses including over 50 small and medium-sized enterprises.
A defence industrial base weighted this heavily towards two frigate programmes is exposed to what happens when they finish, a point made forcefully this week at Ferguson Marine, where the Port Glasgow yard opened a voluntary redundancy programme covering up to 70 staff as work on the ferry Glen Rosa winds down and its BAE Systems subcontract work concludes.
Graeme Downie, the MP whose constituency covers Rosyth, has been pressing the department to confirm that the planned Common Combat Vessel will use the Type 31 hull and be built at the Fife yard, an argument about precisely this problem.
Across the United Kingdom, MOD expenditure with industry totalled £31.9 billion in 2024/25, supporting 274,000 jobs.

Persuasion, denial and bluster: Trump ‘stuck’ on Iran war ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:05 UTC
18:00:05 KST

In the aftermath of his devastating election defeat, the US president remained haunted by regrets over Iran.
Months before Jimmy Carter lost the 1980 presidential election to Ronald Reagan, eight US servicemen died in a botched high-risk rescue mission that failed to secure the freedom of dozens of US hostages seized in Tehran.
As he addressed students and academics, keen for reflections on his single-term presidency, one of the students asked Carter: what do you most regret?
“Not sending more helicopters for the the hostage rescue,” he immediately replied, according to Larry Sabato, director of the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, who hosted the former president. “It was very much on his mind,” said Sabato.
Carter’s fate nearly half a century ago may also be on the mind of Donald Trump as he prepares to embark upon a midterm election campaign over the coming months, while embroiled in a military struggle with Tehran. The Iranian regime is proving equally intractable to that faced by his Democratic predecessor.
Trump’s efforts to finish the war he started along with Israel almost six months ago, on 28 February, have foundered after a ceasefire agreement signed in June collapsed – leaving Iran in control of the strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies before the conflict.
The Iranian stranglehold has pushed up oil prices, stoked inflation and raised living costs in the US, all as Trump’s Republican party already faced an uphill struggle to retain control of US Congress in November’s midterm elections.
With public support for the war running low, polls show a majority of American voters believe they are worse off since Trump returned to office in January 2025. That indicator alone has echoes of Reagan’s famous question to voters during his 1980 presidential debate with Carter: “Are you better off than you were four years ago?”
‘Trump can’t change course’
While the circumstances are different, Trump’s troubles have a broader resemblance to Carter’s dilemma, which began when revolutionaries stormed the US embassy in November 1979 and held 52 diplomats and military personnel hostage.
That was compounded after a daring rescue attempt the following April had to be aborted when three out of eight helicopters deployed on the mission developed mechanical faults. One of the remaining craft collided with a transport plane, killing eight US servicemen and intensifying the ignominy.
Later efforts to negotiate the hostages’ release before the presidential election failed, most notably on the weekend before polling day, when a putative deal collapsed, making Carter’s electoral defeat almost certain.
They were eventually released after 444 days in captivity, minutes after Reagan was sworn into office on 20 January 1981.
The historic parallels are imprecise, but sufficient to be perceived by both Trump and Iran’s current leaders, analysts say.
“Carter couldn’t change course, and maybe that’s what’s most applicable, because Trump can’t change course either,” said Sabato. “Carter was stuck because, after the failed rescue, the hostages were dispersed throughout Iran and there was no way to recover them.
“Trump is stuck because he never had a good rationale [for the war]. He just wanted another victory. All they had to say to Trump to get him to go in was ‘Mr President, this is just going to be another Venezuela, and then we can go in and do Cuba.’”
With a 60-day ceasefire since June’s memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June lapsing this week without any formal resolution, Trump now faces entering an election campaign on the back of an unpopular war that he appears to be losing.
Payback time?
So far, Trump has responded with a mixture of half-hearted persuasion, denial and threatening bluster.
Appearing at the Nassau county police academy in Garden City, New York, on 14 August, he downplayed the war’s impact on fuel prices as necessary to prevent “an evil country” obtaining a nuclear weapon. “Remember that, when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK,” he said.
In an interview with Fox News, he then threatened to “bomb the shit out of” Oman if it “gets in the way” of efforts to end the conflict with Iran. In a futile gesture that drew Iranian mockery, he also declared the strait of Hormuz a “new US territory” on social media.
And in recent days, the president has threatened to unleash “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale” against Iran – omitting details of what precisely this might mean, but vaguely warning countries that provide “any type of lifeline” to Tehran that they, too, will suffer.
The fluctuations seem to betray frustration over a paucity of viable options – a predicament that analysts expect Iran’s leaders to exploit by seeking to deepen Trump’s unpopularity as the midterms approach.
“They are determined to make him pay the consequences of starting this war at the midterm elections,” said Vali Nasr, an Iran expert and international relations professor at Johns Hopkins University.
The approach involves depriving Trump of the option of putting the war on the back burner, or simply declaring victory.
“The whole point Iran is making is that ‘We’re not going to let him decide the sort of ebb and flow of this war,’” said Nasr. “Their position is ‘We have a vote here, and we’re not just going to make it convenient for him’ …
“They have intimated that they are giving him four weeks to go back to the MOU and fully implement it, otherwise they are going to escalate. That means a broader scale of attacks on Gulf targets, more attacks on US bases and US military assets. It’s exactly the opposite of this going low-key, and off the front pages of newspapers.”
The more aggressive Iranian stance has been signaled by a recent shake-up in the regime’s leadership that has included the promotion of Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) for most of the 1980-88 war with Iraq, as secretary of the powerful supreme national security council.
The reshuffle also includes the appointment of Hossein Taeb, a hardline cleric and former intelligence chief, as head of the Basij, a volunteer militia, with a brief to turn it into a neighborhood surveillance unit that will root out domestic opposition and perceived Israeli penetration of Iranian society.
‘Really not in a hurry’
“It’s fair to say that the Iranians have decided that they are going to make life more miserable for Trump in a variety of ways,” said Mehrzad Boroujerdi, a political scientist and vice-provost at Missouri Science and Technology University. “They are certainly going to do whatever they can to hurt him in the midterms.
“Every US public opinion poll I have seen makes a direct correlation with the Iran war and that’s in the minds of the White House in terms of what to do, and the reason we are seeing this switch from Trump threatening military action to basically resigning himself to this idea of the economy being the achilles heel of the Iranian regime, and trying to pressure them to come to the negotiating table.
“But they are really not in a hurry. They do not see the economic condition as that dire for them.”
What may become increasingly dire in the run-up to the midterms is the outlook for the US and global economy, according to Alan Eyre, a former state department Iran specialist, who argued that a race between “two ticking economic clocks” would favor Iran.
“It’s going to get ugly as we head into the midterms,” he said. “We have buffered it to an extent by releasing oil from the strategic petroleum reserve, jawboning the market, and by the Chinese decreasing oil imports, but the resiliency of the system is decreasing significantly and an inflation spike is on the way.”
The driver of a coming economic crunch, argued Eyre, is the rising price of diesel, central to the modern economy because it is the essential fuel in supply chains. “Diesel price is currently $5.44 a gallon. A week ago, $5.30 a gallon. A month ago, $5.06 a gallon. A year ago, $3.70 a gallon,” he said.
Facing an array of bad options, Trump’s only recourse is to choose the least worse – which may also be tantamount to admitting defeat.
“The least bad option is trying to reopen the strait of Hormuz as quickly as possible, as much as possible, under Iranian control, because they are not going to give up control of the strait in the short to mid-term,” said Eyre, who was the state department’s first Farsi-speaking spokesperson under the Obama administration at a time when it was trying to forge stronger ties with Iranian communities across the world.
But Iran is not proffering Trump an olive branch in his hour of need.
‘An electoral wood chipper’?
Even reopening the strait is unlikely to trigger an immediate economic revival as maritime insurance companies take time to assess whether the waterway is safe for ships to use again.
Trump may be oblivious to the electoral fate of members of his own party in US Congress, whom he has treated with scant regard. “He sees his brand as separate and better than the Republican brand,” said Eyre. “And the fact that the Republican party might be walking into an electoral wood chipper in November doesn’t really seem to be motivating him.”
Trump, indeed, may already be preparing for life under a Democratic-controlled Congress. This month he announced the appointment of Will Scharf, a rightwing lawyer, as the new White House legal counsel, with the apparent brief of fighting off an anticipated wave of Democratic demands for subpoenas, documents and congressional investigations.
The president, who publicly refused to accept his defeat to Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election, has also been laying the groundwork to challenge the integrity of November’s poll results, too.
Engineering a electoral drubbing for Trump remains a prize worth pursuing for Iran’s leaders. Such an outcome would set the stage for congressional Democrats to ramp up scrutiny of US conduct in the war.
The outcome of the elections, now less than three months away, “could make the last two years of Trump’s presidency much more difficult for him, and make him much less effective”, said Nasr, of John Hopkins University. “It’s not just the midterms. The day after the elections, all focus will shift to 2028.
“If Trump doesn’t have a way to finish this war, or it becomes nastier with a greater impact on the global economy, then it will begin to become an issue for the presidential election.”
Even that might pale in comparison with the visceral satisfaction a now ageing revolutionary leadership generation would take in delivering a coup de grace reminiscent of that dealt to Carter 46 years ago.
“Why wouldn’t they do the same thing?” asked Sabato, who recalled how Carter reacted with grim resignation when he learned that the last chance of an 11th-hour pre-election deal to free the hostages had collapsed. “They remember the history, and they won then.
“They want to win again against a foe that I’m sure they despise much more than Jimmy Carter. For them, this guy is worse in every way that a human being can be worse.”

Former British and French diplomats urge action over Israel’s ‘erasure’ of Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

More than 100 French and British former diplomats have said Palestine is being erased in front of the world’s eyes and called for urgent action including trade and arms sales bans to press Israel to accept a Palestinian state.
An unprecedented joint letter dispenses with diplomatic language by accusing Israel of ethnic cleansing and warning that the world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy.
Arguing that Britain and France played a key role in the formation of the modern-day Middle East and noting that both countries took the step of recognising Palestine as a state in 2025, the diplomats contend that their countries now have a responsibility “to make common cause on the region’s fundamental fault line – equal rights for Israeli and Palestinians”.
The letter, addressed to the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been signed by 52 French former diplomats and 50 British former ambassadors, many of whom served in the Middle East, in senior posts in Egypt, Iran, Bahrain, Israel, Syria, Turkey, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
The list of British diplomats include two former envoys to the UN, Jeremy Greenstock and Emyr Jones Parry, and a former Foreign Office director of the Middle East, Edward Chaplin. The French signatories include Patrice Paoli, a former Middle East director at the French foreign ministry, and Stanislas de Laboulaye, a former consul general in Jerusalem.
The letter, given to the Guardian and Le Monde, is published two days after the UK and France along with nine other countries condemned the Israeli government’s publication of construction tenders for the E1 settlement project, saying the proposed housing “will take Israel further from peace and undermine its international standing”.
That statement contained no clear threat of consequences apart from a warning to businesses in their jurisdictions not to become involved in bidding since there could be legal and reputational consequences arising from investing in the construction of an unlawful settlement.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, described the tenders for 1,200 homes bisecting the West Bank as a destructive threat to the viability of a two-state solution and summoned the most senior Israeli diplomat currently in the UK, the chargée d’affaires, Daniela Grudsky Ekstein.
In response, Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, vowed Israel would not remain passive, saying the “Jewish people have a right to live throughout Israel just as British people have a right to live throughout the UK”.
The diplomats hope their letter will put pressure on Macron and Burnham to impose specific penalties on Israel in an effort to keep the two-state solution alive.
Diplomacy surrounding the terms for Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza has largely been subcontracted to the negotiations between Israel and Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy, but Israel has rejected the latest 15-point US-led peace plan for Gaza, leading to criticism from eight Muslim countries including the United Arab Emirates, Israel’s closest Muslim ally. They said Israel’s actions “fundamentally undermine the collective efforts undertaken to achieve a just and lasting peace”.
An internal debate has swirled among diplomats over whether the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, through military and political provocations, is seeking to goad countries into reprisals that will help his chances in elections, due on 27 October.
The former diplomats argue the overdue step of recognising Palestine “needs to be made real by urgent action to safeguard the Palestinian right to self-determination, as the Israeli government seeks to destroy any prospect of an independent Palestinian state, showing contempt for the law, the rulings of the international court of justice and countless UN security council resolutions”.
They write: “Our governments care about the security of the Israeli people, just as they are appalled by the suffering of the Palestinian people under occupation. Hamas committed heinous crimes on 7 October 2023, but nothing justifies Israel’s systematic policy of destruction of Gaza and its population. Mr Netanyahu’s assertion that Israel must live by the sword is morally wrong and counterproductive. It imperils Israel’s security and leaves no room for negotiation. As a result, the world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy – there is nothing democratic about depriving others of their rights and land.
“In Gaza, 2 million Palestinians are kettled into 30% of their devastated land, hungry, lacking medicine and housing. Over 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called ‘ceasefire’. In East Jerusalem and the rest of the West Bank, Palestinian house demolitions and rampant settler violence – with the connivance of the Israeli army and police – amount to ethnic cleansing. Palestine is being erased before our eyes. This policy of occupation and destruction extends to Lebanon – where many villages have been razed – and Syria. It is a stain on the conscience of humanity, requiring the UK and France to act.”
They urge the two states to take seven policy steps:
- 
  Uphold the decisions of the international court of justice and the international criminal court.
- 
  Suspend the EU-Israel association agreement and the UK-Israel trade and partnership agreement for breach of human rights provisions.
- 
  Suspend arms transfers to and from Israel and all bilateral military cooperation.
- 
  Insist on unrestricted aid access to Gaza, led by the UN Relief and Works Agency, other UN agencies and international NGOs, with consequences for non-compliance, and access too for journalists, diplomats and parliamentarians.
- 
  Ban all trade with settlements, including goods, investment, insurance and other financial services.
- 
  Warn potential bidders for the “red line” E1 settlement or other settlement financing/construction that their interests in and with the UK and France will suffer.
- 
  Make it an offence for British and French citizens to buy property on stolen Palestinian land and remove charitable status from “charities” funding settlements.
The diplomats balance their criticism of Israel by saying Palestinians “have to ensure that the state recognised by over two-thirds of the world is democratic and law-abiding, despite the occupation. Gaza and the West Bank need to be reunited politically, administratively and economically. Palestine’s political leadership is unrepresentative and dysfunctional. The elections in November [in Palestine] must lead to democratic renewal.”
But they argue: “While our two governments can do much to help Palestine to be a fully functioning democratic nation, the focus needs to be on Israel’s determination to prevent that outcome.”
The Israeli embassy in London was contacted for comment.

Living in fear, and not being paid: the health workers on the frontline of DRC’s Ebola outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:04 UTC
18:00:04 KST

Every day, Sophie Mwadawa Kabundo goes to her job as a nurse at an Ebola treatment centre in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, afraid she will contract the virus and pass it to her family and friends.
“More and more confirmed cases are being admitted here … Some of our colleagues have died,” said Kabundo. “We fear that, despite our vigilance, workplace accidents may occur and put us in ever greater danger … We go to sleep already worrying about the days ahead, as patients continue to pour in.”
Martin Bolombi, her colleague at the Elikya treatment centre in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit province, Ituri, holds similar fears. “Personally, this outbreak is causing me a lot of stress,” he said. “But I have no choice but to pluck up my courage and ensure that the situation is brought under control first, before it can stabilise.”
That courage is all the more remarkable given that both workers on the frontline of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record said they were not being paid.
“I have been working since May and have only been paid for June,” said Bolombi, a hygiene worker who was among about 100 people who protested outside the Elikya treatment centre during a strike last month over unpaid bonuses.
Kabundo said she was also missing wages. “We are not being paid and we want the government to provide solutions as soon as possible,” she said. “We are under immense pressure … We are exposed to the risk of infection, and our families and other loved ones may contract the disease because of us.”
Unpaid wages are just one of the factors – alongside misinformation, community mistrust and infrastructure deficits – hampering efforts to tackle the outbreak in the DRC, one of the world’s poorest countries.
More than 2,500 people have now died in the outbreak, which is spreading exponentially in an area larger than France, the senior UN Ebola coordinator, Julien Harneis, said on Friday. Speaking on a video call from Bunia, Harneis called for more aid, saying the existing pool of funds would run out within weeks. He said 160 healthcare workers had fallen ill with Ebola, and 43 of them had died.
“The outbreak is growing faster and wider than the Ebola response,” he added. “And all of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs.”
The World Health Organization estimates that the outbreak is on course to exceed west Africa’s 2014-16 Ebola outbreak as the biggest ever globally. In the previous outbreak, more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths were recorded across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to WHO data.
The infections in DRC are of the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for the strain, but trials for both are under way.
Bolombi said he was working seven days a week, with barely any time to see his family, as the outbreak was getting worse. “Logistics have improved compared to the early days of the response, but this is still not enough, as needs are growing as the disease progresses,” he said.
Despite the enormous challenges and lack of renumeration, Kabundo expressed pride that there had been “a large number of recoveries” at the Elikya treatment centre. “This progress must be highlighted, but it is no excuse to rest on our laurels,” she said.
The Congolese health ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ebola is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads between humans via direct contact with the organs, blood or other body fluids of infected people, including dead bodies. It can also be spread through contact with contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding or clothing.
Initial symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headaches and a sore throat. These progress to vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.
Widespread mistrust and misinformation have resulted in people with the virus not attending health centres for treatment until it is too late, as well as attacks on health facilities and ambulances.
Dr Eddy Kambale Kahandukya, a deputy medical coordinator for the charity Médicins Sans Frontières in the DRC, said: “The lack of community engagement remains a major challenge in breaking this chain of transmission … For example, patients who suspect they have symptoms and are awaiting laboratory results seek refuge within the community and end up creating new clusters that further fuel the spread of the epidemic.”
Fear was a big driver of the lack of trust in the authorities’ response to Ebola, said Manon Dumortier, an emergency coordinator in Bunia for the aid group Mercy Corps.
“It’s scary, right? … Suddenly there are so many people dying and you don’t know what it is about,” she said. “People are just disappearing, going to health centres and you cannot even see them before they are being buried. This is just raising a lot of speculation and rumours.”
The WHO declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern in May, but later said sequencing showed the outbreak had started months earlier in February.
The virus has spread to six of the DRC’s 26 provinces, concentrated in the country’s north-east. More than 4,200 of the confirmed cases are in Ituri, which borders Uganda and South Sudan.
Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths, all in the capital, Kampala. The government declared the country Ebola-free on 28 July after the last Ebola patient, a Congolese national, was discharged on 16 July.

Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:03 UTC
18:00:03 KST

Despite this summer bringing hours of sunshine, many Britons have been unable to cash in on free electricity generated by the sun. Rooftop solar panels are usually out of the question if you live in a flat or rent your home, and the cost has made them prohibitive to many more households.
However, this could be about to change because next week the first wave of low-cost “plug-in” solar panels will go on sale in Great Britain.
Also known as “plug‑and‑play” or “balcony” solar, the clue to what makes them different is in the name: you can fix them to a balcony or garden wall, then plug them in like a toaster.
The mini solar systems are a familiar sight on balconies in Spain and in Germany, where they are known as a Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant), but until a recent change in the law, they were not permitted in Britain.
Matt Parry from the Renewable Energy Association, a trade body for renewable energy, says the kits are a gamechanger. “It democratises solar and gives everyone the chance to get it,” he says.
How the kits work
Unlike traditional rooftop solar panels, which require a professional to install, balcony solar kits – which commonly include one or two panels – can be plugged in to a three-prong wall socket.
You can fix them on a balcony railing, shed roof or garden wall – anywhere with good sun exposure and safe access.
When sunlight hits the solar panels, they generate a direct current. The microinverter then converts this to an alternating current, which flows into your home’s electrical system, reducing the amount you draw from the grid.
Previously, rules around the installation of solar were what was holding people back. But last year the government announced it would make it possible for plug-in solar to be used in this country.
To make this a reality, it has updated wiring regulations to allow households in Great Britain to connect plug-in solar panels capable of generating up to 800 watts of power into the mains without the need for an electrician. (The rules are different in Northern Ireland.)
Buying panels
Big names including B&Q, Currys, Lidl, Wickes and Amazon are lining up to sell plug-in solar.
Given the size (and weight) of these devices, it is expected that many will be bought online.
Although you may have already come across plug-in solar panels for sale, industry experts suggest waiting until the regulations take effect on 27 August before making a purchase.
Electrical Safety First, the consumer safety charity, is urging shoppers to stick to reputable high street retailers and their websites to ensure the device complies with the rules.
Luke Osborne, the charity’s technical director, advises people to “avoid buying these devices from third-party sellers on online marketplaces. These platforms are now not legally responsible for the safety of goods sold via their sites, exposing people to substandard versions that may put you and your home at risk.”
Andrew Moore, the founder of the British solar panel brand UKSOL, says: “We are working towards making the initial products available from 27 August.”
His company will initially sell 460W and 890W kits, starting at £599 and £999 respectively, and it plans to launch another four models in late September, with prices starting from £499.
Sizewise, plug-in solar setups are usually smaller than rooftop options, but sizes vary. The UKSOL 460W single panel kit measures 1,762mm x 1,134mm x 30mm and weighs 25.5kg. The 890W kit comprises two panels.
Setting up
The official guidance suggests that it will take about an hour to set up your system. It estimates 15-25% of people will need professional support mounting the panels, and about 15% will need minor electrical works. UKSOL suggests it takes two people to handle and position the panels, as each one weighs 25kg.
Osborne says plug-in solar systems should not be connected via extension leads, cable reels, multiway adaptors, travel adaptors or plug-in RCD adaptors. “These accessories can overheat, become overloaded and create additional safety risks,” he says.
There is also some other housekeeping. The owner has to tell their distribution network operator that they are using them (there should be a form in the box). You can find out who it is by inputting your postcode on the Energy Networks Association website. You will also be able to consult the ENA’s Connect Direct site for a list of approved devices, which is a good place to start before you buy.
Savings
Plug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system, which means they will not provide enough energy to power a home on their own – but they could cut your bill.
One drawback is that you need to be home to use the power generated because without a battery it is not being stored for later, so flows back to the grid.
However, the adoption of balcony solar could, in time, pave the way for plug-in batteries in British homes, too. If paired with a plug-in solar system, households could store their own renewable electricity during the day and use it to run their appliances in the evenings. The government is reportedly considering plans to bulk-buy the devices and distribute them to low-income homes.
A basic plug-in solar system costs about £400. Parry says it will “give you back, at worst, £40 a year, and at the best about £110. If it’s the worst-case scenario, it’s going to pay for itself in 10 years, but at the best-case scenario, it’s four.
“If you’ve just got 800W, it’s only at its very peak that it will give you that.”
He adds: “The slight downside is that plug-in solar is hitting the markets as the summer’s coming to an end. It’s going to be more use in May next year.”
Moore says that the level of saving is affected by a number of things, including the system size, location, orientation and actually being home to use the power.
He expects the 460W system his company will be selling to save a typical household about £80-£120 a year, “while the 890W system could save more”.
He adds: “The greatest savings are achieved when households use appliances during daylight hours, as this increases the proportion of generated electricity used within the home.”
You can buy a more expensive 2,000W kit (the inverter will only allow 800W through) to maximise your power-generating capacity, but these are more expensive.
Staying safe
Although there is no obligation to do this, before buying a kit, some experts think you should get your home electrics checked by a professional. That is because this is the first time that British residential wiring circuits will take power in via a three-point socket rather than simply being used to distribute electricity.
Electrical Safety First is concerned about the impact on residual current devices, or RCDs, which sit in a household electricity box and cut off the power if someone drills through a wire or runs their lawnmower over a power cord. Electricians are concerned they may burn out when plug-in solar panels start adding electricity to the circuit.
A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson says: “Plug-in solar panels will be available to buy this summer, and stringent verification and registration checks are already in place. They are a transformative technology that can save people hundreds of pounds on their bills.”
Box] Renters
Plug-in solar should make it easier for tenants to take advantage of renewable energy, as any kit they buy can be moved from place to place.
But if you are renting, you should ask permission from your landlord before you invest in any panels.
The rules on what you can do with regard to fixing brackets to hold them, for example, may vary depending on what your tenancy agreement says.
There’s “no reason” why your landlord should be against the idea, Parry says. “He or she can look at the information and know it’s super, super safe.”
Meera Chindooroy, the deputy director of campaigns, public affairs and policy at the National Residential Landlords Association, says that while the organisation supports the “principle of tenants benefiting from plug-in solar panels … landlords would first need to be satisfied that the panels meet all required safety standards”.
She adds: “It would not be right for landlords to be held responsible for the safety of equipment they were not asked about in the first place.”

NASA Cancels Its Rescue Mission for the Aging Swift Telescope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The Swift space observatory has been in operation since 2004. It specializes in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most energetic electromagnetic explosions known in the universe. Its original mission was supposed to last just two years. More than two decades later, it continues to explore some of the most violent phenomena in the cosmos. Now it is nearing the end of its life.
Swift doesn’t have a propulsion system capable of significantly raising its orbit. Although it is hundreds of kilometers above the Earth’s surface, there are still atmospheric particles at that altitude that exert a small but constant drag on the satellite. With each orbit around Earth, it loses a tiny amount of energy and, little by little, altitude as well. If this process continues without intervention it will eventually reenter the atmosphere.
NASA knew that Swift had limited time left. Some models had indicated that the observatory could remain in orbit until the 2030s, but increased solar activity during 2024 changed those projections. Energy from the sun heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Estimates eventually placed its likely reentry before the end of 2026.
Faced with the rapid deterioration of Swift’s orbit, NASA decided to attempt a rescue maneuver straight out of a movie. The plan was simple in concept but astonishingly complex to execute. A robotic mission would catch up to Swift, capture it with mechanical arms, and use its own thrusters to raise the observatory to a safer orbit, where it could continue operating. To do this, NASA turned to the company Katalyst Space Technologies and its LINK spacecraft.
LINK was launched into space on July 3, 2026. However, problems arose soon after. The spacecraft suffered failures in its attitude control system, which is responsible for keeping it properly oriented and stable in space. For weeks, engineers worked to regain control.
On Wednesday, NASA canceled the rescue mission. In a statement, agency administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the decision was due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system. LINK will no longer capture Swift or raise its orbit. The spacecraft will continue to approach the observatory to conduct demonstrations of rendezvous, navigation, and close-proximity operations. The agency hopes to use this attempt to gather information that can be applied to future missions aimed at repairing, relocating, or extending the lifespan of satellites in orbit.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow,” Isaacman said in a press release.
The agency had warned from the outset that this was a high-risk mission. Swift was not built to be captured or repaired in orbit, while LINK was developed and launched against the clock in response to the observatory’s rapid descent.
“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” Isaacman noted.
Without an intervention to raise its orbit, Swift will continue to lose altitude until it reaches the denser layers of the atmosphere. During reentry, much of the observatory will be destroyed by intense heating and aerodynamic forces. It is still too early to determine exactly when and where this will occur.
For now, NASA estimates that Swift will likely reenter the atmosphere before the end of the year.

Moped mania: chasing teenage kicks at 30km/h
Unknown
