Caffeine might ease anxiety and depression by calming brain inflammation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
16:00:37 UTC
01:00:37 KST

Caffeine appears to alleviate symptoms of anxiety and depression in rodents by reducing inflammation in the brain. A recent systematic review of 17 animal studies found that the widely consumed stimulant consistently diminished behavioral signs of distress and lowered levels of inflammatory molecules. The findings were published in Translational Psychiatry.
Mental health conditions like anxiety and depression involve physical changes in the nervous system. Over the past few decades, researchers have identified neuroinflammation as a major contributor to these mood disorders. When the body experiences chronic psychological stress or illness, the immune system often responds by releasing proteins called cytokines.
These cytokines travel to the brain and activate specialized immune cells known as microglia and astrocytes. Once activated, these glial cells can disrupt the normal balance of neurotransmitters like dopamine and serotonin. This inflammatory process can trigger behaviors associated with mood disorders, such as a loss of motivation or heightened fear responses.
Caffeine is a psychoactive substance that primarily works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain. Adenosine is a chemical that naturally accumulates during the day, binding to specific receptors to promote sleepiness. By blocking these receptors, caffeine keeps the brain alert.
Adenosine receptors are not just involved in wakefulness. A specific subtype, called the A2A receptor, is prominently featured on the surface of microglia and astrocytes. Prolonged stress can cause an overabundance of these A2A receptors, which makes the brain’s immune cells highly sensitive and prone to causing inflammation.
Because caffeine blocks these A2A receptors, scientists suspect it might act as a brake on the brain’s inflammatory response. Neurobiologists Laís da Silva Neves and Paula Campello-Costa at the Fluminense Federal University in Brazil wanted to synthesize the existing data on this topic. Along with their colleagues, they set out to analyze how caffeine influences both brain inflammation and behavior in animal models.
The research team conducted a systematic review, a process that involves collecting and evaluating all the published scientific literature on a specific research question. They combed through online databases and identified 17 rodent studies that met their strict inclusion criteria. Every selected study featured a control group to allow for objective comparisons.
The team first looked at six studies focusing on anxiety. In these experiments, researchers induced anxiety in adult rats through various stressful scenarios. These included acute stressors, like a brief period of sleep deprivation or exposure to the scent of a predator, as well as chronic stressors, such as repeated physical restraint.
During or after these stressful events, the rodents received caffeine. The method of administration varied by study. Some animals received the substance through their drinking water, while others were given direct injections or fed through a gastric tube.
Scientists then measured the animals’ anxiety levels using established behavioral tests. A common method involves placing the rodent in an elevated, cross-shaped maze with both open and enclosed arms. Anxious animals will generally hide in the dark, enclosed arms, while less anxious animals will spend more time exploring the exposed sections.
Neves, Campello-Costa, and their team noted that caffeine consistently promoted exploratory behaviors, indicating a reduction in anxiety. This behavioral shift was accompanied by distinct physical changes in the animals’ brains. The rodents treated with caffeine exhibited lower levels of oxidative stress, a type of cellular damage associated with psychological strain.
Brain tissue analysis also revealed a drop in several pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. At the same time, the caffeine-treated animals showed increased levels of anti-inflammatory molecules. The substance effectively prevented the microglia and astrocytes from entering a highly reactive, damaging state.
The remaining eleven studies in the review focused on animal models of depression. To mimic the biological mechanisms of depression, researchers in several of these studies injected the mice or rats with lipopolysaccharide. This molecule is a structural component of bacterial cell walls, and injecting it tricks the animal’s immune system into launching a massive, body-wide inflammatory response.
Other depression models utilized chronic unpredictable mild stress or long-term sleep deprivation. To assess whether the animals had entered a depressive-like state, researchers used tests that measure motivation and the capacity to experience pleasure. For example, they tracked whether the rodents lost interest in drinking sweetened water, a behavior that mirrors the loss of pleasure seen in human depression.
Across the different models, caffeine administration protected the rodents from developing these depressive-like behaviors. The animals maintained their motivation in physical tests and continued to seek out rewards like sugar water. In some of the studies, caffeine performed just as well as standard antidepressant medications like imipramine.
When examining the biological data from these depression models, the reviewers found a similar pattern to the anxiety studies. Caffeine reversed the chemical changes induced by the bacterial components or the chronic stress. The treated rodents displayed higher levels of protective antioxidant enzymes and fewer inflammatory markers in regions of the brain associated with memory and emotion.
A few of the evaluated studies also tested substances closely related to caffeine, such as caffeic acid and green tea extract. These compounds provided similar mood-boosting and anti-inflammatory benefits. Some research even suggested that standard caffeinated coffee and decaffeinated coffee both lowered inflammation, though the behavioral benefits were sometimes tied strictly to the caffeine.
While the review points to a robust anti-inflammatory effect, translating these findings to humans requires caution. Animal models can replicate specific neurochemical mechanisms, but they cannot capture the subjective, conscious experience of human anxiety or depression. The behavioral tests only act as proxies for actual mood disorders.
Almost all the studies in this review used adult male rodents. This uniformity makes the data easier to pool and compare, but it leaves a major gap in the scientific literature. It remains unknown if caffeine produces the exact same neuroinflammatory responses in female rodents or in animals at different developmental stages, such as adolescents or the elderly.
The amount of caffeine administered in these experiments also varied widely. Some doses were relatively low, mimicking the concentration a human might get from a standard cup of coffee. Other studies used extremely high doses that would be toxic to humans.
One study in the review actually demonstrated that a massive dose of caffeine worsened anxiety and increased brain inflammation in sleep-deprived rats. High doses of stimulants are known to trigger panic and hyperactivity in both humans and animals. Future research will need to determine the exact doses and consumption habits required to safely harness caffeine’s anti-inflammatory properties for mental health treatments.
The study, “Effects of caffeine on neuroinflammation in anxiety and depression: a systematic review of rodent studies,” was authored by Laís da Silva Neves, Giovanna Várzea Roberti Monteiro de Mattos, Yasmin Oliveira-Nazareth, Rosane Souza da Silva, and Paula Campello-Costa.

Iran calls for binding treaty to prevent an arms race in outer space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:58:50 UTC
00:58:50 KST

Iran calls for binding treaty to prevent an arms race in outer space
TEHRAN- Iran has called for the immediate start of negotiations on a comprehensive, legally binding international treaty to prevent an arms race in outer space, warning that the growing militarization of space poses a serious threat to international security and the peaceful use of space technologies.
Addressing the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva on Thursday, Iran’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office and other international organizations, Ali Bahreini, said the increasing dependence of societies on space-based technologies had made the security and sustainability of outer space a shared international concern.
Bahreini said Iran remained committed to preserving outer space exclusively for peaceful purposes and argued that the deployment of weapons and offensive military capabilities in space could undermine international peace and security and threaten the equal right of all countries to explore and use outer space for peaceful purposes.
Iran expressed particular concern over the development of military space programs and capabilities, including the establishment of dedicated military space forces, the designation of outer space as a war-fighting domain and initiatives such as the so-called “Golden Dome.” Bahreini warned that efforts by individual states to establish military superiority in space could prompt other countries to develop counter-capabilities, creating cycles of escalation and increasing the risk of an arms race.
Tehran also raised concerns over 'the increasingly hostile use of large satellite constellations, commercial satellites and other space-based systems.' Bahreini said international humanitarian law should not be applied in ways that could provide undue protection to commercial satellite networks when they are used for hostile purposes or in ways that infringe on the sovereignty of states.
Iran further argued that international protections should extend beyond objects in orbit to ground-based infrastructure that supports peaceful space activities. Bahreini said research and production facilities, launch sites, operational and monitoring centers, as well as civilian and scientific infrastructure supporting essential space services, should not be subject to military attack.
He accused the United States and Israel of targeting civilian and scientific infrastructure associated with Iran’s peaceful space activities during 'the recent full-scale war against Iran.'
According to Bahreini, the facilities supported disaster management, environmental monitoring, satellite communications, scientific research, public warning systems and emergency services.
Iran condemned the attacks and warned that a failure by the international community to respond could leave other states vulnerable to similar actions.
“Space security must not be defined solely from the perspective of technologically advanced countries,” Bahreini said, arguing that developing countries have the same right to security in their peaceful use of outer space.
Iran therefore called for the immediate commencement of negotiations at the Conference on Disarmament on a comprehensive, non-discriminatory and legally binding international instrument to prevent an arms race in outer space, commonly known as PAROS.
Tehran said such an agreement should prohibit the placement of weapons in outer space, prevent the threat or use of force from space against states or space objects, ban the use of space-based capabilities for hostile and offensive military purposes, and provide effective protection for peaceful civilian space infrastructure.
Bahreini said Iran regarded a draft treaty submitted by Russia and China in 2008 and updated in 2014 as a useful basis for future negotiations. The proposed framework seeks to prevent the placement of weapons in outer space and prohibit the threat or use of force against space objects.
Iran also rejected the idea that voluntary measures alone could adequately address the growing security risks in space. Bahreini said measures such as responsible-behavior norms, risk-reduction mechanisms and operational or technological restraint could complement a legally binding agreement but could not replace one.
“PAROS is an urgent security imperative,” Bahreini said, calling on states to move beyond fragmented and non-binding approaches and demonstrate the political will to begin negotiations without further delay.
Iran said any future agreement should also promote equitable and non-discriminatory access to outer space, space technologies and related capabilities, particularly for developing countries, while safeguarding their right to benefit from the peaceful uses of space.

What you need to know about West Nile virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:57:59 UTC
00:57:59 KST

Hundreds of people across the U.S. have been sickened with a mosquito-borne illness that can cause flulike symptoms, debilitating headaches and, in rare cases, even brain swelling.
This week New York City reported its first human case of West Nile virus for the year; health officials said the infected individual may have contracted the virus outside of the city. But officials have found West Nile virus in mosquitoes across every borough of New York City this summer—and that’s not unusual.
West Nile virus is the most common mosquito-borne illness in the U.S. The latest Centers for Disease Control and Prevention update reports 222 human cases this year across 32 states, with the highest counts in Arizona, Texas and California. Most infections are asymptomatic or cause flulike symptoms that could be confused with a common cold, meaning that the true number of infections is likely far higher.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But in some cases, West Nile can reach the brain and cause extreme headaches, meningitis, tremors, convulsions and paralysis. In very rare instances, West Nile can cause brain swelling, or encephalitis.
Summer and fall tends to mean a lot of time spent outdoors, in nature and around mosquitoes. And while this year hasn’t seen unusually high West Nile case numbers so far, it’s important to try to avoid mosquito bites altogether because no vaccine exists for the virus if you do contract it.
Culex mosquitoes are the most common carrier of the virus. These insects live all over the country and often thrive in populated environments. Some areas and cities, including New York, spray pesticides to try to prevent the spread of the virus. But health experts also recommend covering bare skin, employing mosquito nets and using insect repellent, especially at night, when mosquito bites most often occur.
The CDC recommends using insect repellents that are registered with the Environmental Protection Agency and have active ingredients such as DEET, oil of lemon eucalyptus or picaridin. If you are also using sunscreen, apply it first and put on the insect repellent second.
Air-conditioning and screens on windows and doors can also help keep mosquitoes out of your home, as can making sure there is no standing water where the insects can lay their eggs.

Why this El Niño will be the largest in living memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:57:31 UTC
00:57:31 KST

The already superlative El Niño that began earlier this year is looking to be the largest El Niño in living memory and likely the strongest since the 19th century, the U.K. Met Office reports.
“We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event,” said Adam Scaife, the Met Office’s head of long-range forecasting, in a statement. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.”
El Niño is a cyclical climate phenomenon where a “warm pool” in the tropical Pacific shifts from its usual spot in the west to the east. This El Niño has steadily gained steam since it was declared in early June, setting a sea surface temperature record for that time of year. And because El Niño typically peaks in late fall to early winter, this event is likely to be a blockbuster.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
During an El Niño, temperatures in the eastern tropical Pacific generally rise by about one to two degrees Celsius (1.8 to 3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, “with 2o C being a really big event,” Scaife said. This year’s event is predicted to hit around three degrees C (5.4 degrees F) above normal, well into the territory of what is colloquially termed a “Super El Niño.” If that forecast bears out, “then 2026 will far exceed our recent experience of El Niño and its worldwide climate influences,” he added. The most recent very strong El Niños occurred in 1982–1983, 1997–1998 and 2015–2016.
El Niño changes the weather around the world by adjusting where heat is released into the atmosphere, which alters major wind patterns. In fact, this event has already juiced Hurricane Lala, whose rainfall devastated Hawaii (though it is keeping a lid on Atlantic hurricane activity) and has contributed to well-below-normal rainfall from the Indian monsoon.
The strength of this El Niño could cause 2026 to become the hottest year on record—it will certainly be among the hottest years. But 2027 may be more likely to take the top slot because the effects of El Niño’s heat release happen on a delay. (Both 1998 and 2016 were record hot years, but both have since fallen down the rankings as climate change has made record hot years more likely.) Either way, 2027 will probably be “another year to temporarily exceed +1.5 C above the preindustrial period,” the Met Office’s Nick Dunstone said in the statement.

Texas Tech seeks Big 12 repeat while BYU among teams trying to be 7th different champ in 7 seasons
The Big 12 Conference has had six different champions in the past six seasons.
While 12th-ranked Texas Tech seeks a repeat after winning its first Big 12 title and making the College Football Playoff, teams like No. 14 BYU, No. 21 Utah and No. 23 Houston could make a push to extend the league’s streak to seven.
“We want to do something that very few teams have been able to do, and that’s to win the Big 12 championship again,” Tech coach Joey McGuire said.
The Red Raiders reloaded again through the transfer portal after setting school records with 12 wins and nine NFL draft picks. Will Hammond is healthy after an ACL injury last season and will start at quarterback after the offseason legal saga surrounding transfer Brendan Sorsby, who was declared ineligible by the NCAA because of gambling.
BYU is coming off its first 12-win season since 2001, and both its losses were to Texas Tech, 29-7 in Lubbock, then 34-7 in the Big 12 title game.
“We know that last year was some really cool things, some awesome success,” 11th-year Cougars coach Kalani Sitake said. “At the same time, we know what we can do better.”
The Cougars return Big 12 rushing leader LJ Martin (1,305 yards, 12 TDs rushing) and QB Bear Bachmeier, who threw for 3,033 yards, ran for 527 and accounted for 26 TDs (15 passing, 11 rushing) after getting thrust into the starting role as a true freshman.
Houston went from four wins to 10 in its second season with coach Willie Fritz, and returns dual-threat QB Conner Weigman (3,405 total yards and 36 TDs.) Utah has 82% of its total offense back (QBs Devon Dampier and Byrd Ficklin, and RB Wayshawn Parker) from an 11-win team, but two offensive linemen were first-round NFL draft picks and coach Kyle Whittingham left after 22 seasons for Michigan.
Out West in the desert and the Rockies
Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita, that national active leader with 73 TD passes, is a rarity going into his fourth season starting for the same team. With him back and the unexpected return of leading rusher Ismail Mahdi, the Wildcats hope to build on a 9-4 finish and be a Big 12 contender.
Arizona State won the Big 12 title and made the playoff in its league debut in 2024. The injury-plagued Sun Devils weren’t able to repeat last year and now are without QB Sam Leavitt (transfer to LSU) and receiver Jordyn Tyson (first-round NFL pick by New Orleans).
Deion Sanders, who last year had surgery for bladder cancer, said he feels like his old self going into his fourth season at Colorado. He hired new offensive and defensive coordinators after a five-game losing streak to end last season with a 1-8 conference record. He is 16-21 overall with the Buffs.
There are four new coaches in the Big 12, with some familiar faces
The Big 12’s four new head coaches include Kansas State’s Collin Klein and Utah’s Morgan Scalley at their alma maters replacing their former bosses. Jimmy Rogers took over at Iowa State when Matt Campbell left after 10 seasons for Penn State, and Eric Morris is at Oklahoma State.
Klein had been gone for two seasons as Texas A&M’s offensive coordinator when Chris Klieman suddenly retired from K-State. Scalley was Utah’s defensive coordinator when Whittingham resigned. Roger won an FCS national championship three seasons ago as head coach at his alma mater, South Dakota State, and was at Washington State last year.
Oklahoma State’s 88 newcomers include 21 who came with Morris from North Texas, which lost to Tulane in the American Conference championship game to miss out on a CFP berth. Among the Mean Green transfers were QB Drew Mestemaker, the national passing leader with 4,379 yards as a freshman, RB Caleb Hawkins (1,434 yards and FBS-best 25 TDs rushing as a freshman) and WR Wyatt Young (70 catches, 1,264 yards, 10 TDs).
This is the first time since 2004 the Cowboys enter a season without Mike Gundy their head coach. They have lost 19 conference games in a row, with consecutive 0-9 conference records since a 49-21 loss to Texas in the 2023 Big 12 championship game.
The Big 12 needs to make a playoff statement
After making the 12-team playoff and getting a first-round bye last season, Texas Tech lost 23-0 to Oregon in the Orange Bowl quarterfinal game. That dropped the Big 12, which has never had multiple playoff teams, to 1-8 in CFP games.
“There’s an obligation as programs in this conference that we play at a high level, and then I think it’s really important that we win in the playoffs,” McGuire said. “Until we do that as a conference, then we’re going to continue to have the same narrative that we have right now.”
The Big 12’s last repeat champion is no longer in the league
Oklahoma won a record 14 Big 12 championships before going to the SEC two years ago. The Sooners won six in a row from 2015 to 2020, followed by Baylor, Kansas State, Texas, Arizona State and the Red Raiders winning titles.
This will be the 31st season for the Big 12, which will host its 25th championship game Dec. 4.

Ex-Abercrombie &amp; Fitch CEO is mentally fit for sex trafficking trial, judge says

Ex-Abercrombie & Fitch CEO is mentally fit for sex trafficking trial, judge says
NEW YORK (AP) — The former CEO of Abercrombie & Fitch is mentally competent to stand trial as he faces sex trafficking charges after being hospitalized for months for dementia and Alzheimer’s symptoms, a federal judge ruled.
U.S. District Court Judge Nusrat Choudhury, in her Thursday decision, concluded that Michael Jeffries “clearly possesses a rational and factual understanding of the proceedings” and is a “reasonably intelligent person and skilled communicator” following his stay at a federal prison hospital in Butner, North Carolina.
The federal judge on Long Island, New York, said she reviewed testimony and written reports from medical experts and listened to hours of phone calls Jeffries made to his romantic partner, lawyers and others while in custody.
“His presentation and responses in evaluations following his commitment to Butner and his phone calls show that he understands the structure of the criminal legal system, courtroom procedures, the functions of the various participants, the nature and purpose of the proceedings, and key legal concepts,” Choudhury wrote.
Jeffries’ lawyer declined to comment.
“We do not comment on the Judge’s rulings,” Brian Bieber wrote in an email. “The case, and all related issues, will be tried inside the courtroom – not in the media.”
Jeffries, 82, is currently free on bond. He’s slated to go on trial in late October, alongside two co-defendants, his partner Matthew Smith and staffer James Jacobson. A pretrial hearing is slated for next Thursday.
Jeffries’ lawyers had argued that he required around-the-clock care to deal with the effects of Alzheimer’s disease, Lewy body dementia and a traumatic brain injury. They had medical experts testify in court that Jeffries’ cognitive issues were “progressive and incurable” and that he would not “regain his competency.”
That prompted Choudhury to order Jeffries to be hospitalized to see if his mental condition would improve. After spending about four months at Butner, federal prison officials in December deemed Jeffries mentally fit to stand trial.
Jeffries, Smith and Jacobson have pleaded not guilty to federal charges, including sex trafficking and interstate prostitution.
Prosecutors say the three used the promise of modeling jobs to lure men to drug-fueled sex parties in New York City, the Hamptons and other locations. The criminal case echoes sexual misconduct accusations made in a civil case and in the media in recent years.
Jeffries left Abercrombie in 2014 after more than two decades. He’s credited with transforming the New York retailer, originally founded to sell wilderness gear, into a mainstay of teen mall culture in the early 2000s with its preppy youth aesthetic and sexy marketing.

From rural routes to desegregation runs, the yellow school bus faces a new reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:53:02 UTC
00:53:02 KST

From rural routes to desegregation runs, the yellow school bus faces a new reality
CHICAGO (AP) — They arrived in a kaleidoscope of colors, but one won. For decades, the American school bus has maintained such a standard look that “school bus yellow” is national shorthand for their deep, glossy hue.
No act of Congress mandated the color, with its slight orange tint. Rather, a 1939 conference of transportation officials from all U.S. states (then 48) chose the shade for its visibility as one of the first safety standards. At their peak in the 1980s, the yellow buses took more than 60% of U.S. students to school.
The metal-bodied school bus got its start in rural America. Georgia car dealer Albert Luce designed it to carry cement workers, then marketed it to schools when the company turned it down.
It was impeccable timing as school districts replaced one-room neighborhood schoolhouses with larger ones much farther apart. That consolidation gave rise to the school bus.
“I don’t think you could’ve had one without the other,” says Matt Anderson, head transportation curator at the Henry Ford Museum of American Innovation in Dearborn, Michigan, which houses Luce’s 1927 bus.
Decades later, buses helped desegregate schools, hauling Black and white children across the country’s racial divide. The controversial practice has mostly ended, and in much of the United States, schools have grown more segregated, not less.
Carl Fisher drove a metal school bus for two-thirds of its nearly 100-year history. With 66 years behind the wheel, Fisher retired in 2012 as the longest-working driver, according to the Guinness Book of World Records. His first model was a Dodge truck that his dad’s friend converted, adding benches and small stools to haul 20 children in Pleasant Hope, Missouri.
“He put windows in it and everything, really made it nice,” Fisher says.
The basics became industry standard and more safety upgrades followed, including padded seats and a flip-out stop sign.
“It’s the safest form of on-road transportation per passenger, per mile, bar none — without seat belts,” says Brad Beauchamp, who is with the electric vehicles team at Blue Bird, the yellow school bus maker Luce reputedly named after the bird his wife spotted on a fence post.
Due to driver shortages and other factors, a yellow school bus is no longeravailable to take many students to school, putting pressure on families to figure out transportation.
Jim Oppegard, who drove kids for more than two decades in the Minneapolis suburb of Brooklyn Park, retired at 94 as the oldest school bus driver on record. It’s rewarding work, he says.
“You’re helping the kids and helping the overall society,” he says. “You’re doing an important job.”

School attendance has bounced back in Connecticut. Leaders hail LEAP program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:53:02 UTC
00:53:02 KST

School attendance has bounced back in Connecticut. Leaders hail LEAP program
It began in 2021, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic: an effort, backed by federal dollars from the American Rescue Plan Act, to get Connecticut students back in school amid a spike in chronic absenteeism. The strategy: send volunteers directly into homes to build relationships with families, connect them with resources and, they hoped, improve attendance.
Five years later, state leaders and national experts on school attendance have declared the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program, or LEAP, a resounding success. In the 2021-2022 school year, chronic absenteeism in Connecticut reached 23.7%, nearly double what it was pre-COVID. This past school year, it dropped to 16.4% — a decrease of roughly 35,000 students. That’s still higher than before the pandemic but well below the 2021 peak.
Gov. Ned Lamont, whose administration has overseen LEAP from its creation to the present day, said he’s pleased with the results.
“This is a program that I think is working,” Lamont told a large crowd of educators, LEAP home visitors and state officials at a gathering on Wednesday to celebrate LEAP’s five-year anniversary.
LEAP operates as a partnership between the state of Connecticut, its Regional Education Service Centers and local community organizations. Pairs of trained home visitors visit families with children at risk of chronic absenteeism. Over several months, the home visitors build relationships with the families, identifying why the kids aren’t going to school and offering resources.
LEAP home visitor Cecelia Garay said the causes of missing school vary.
“Some of the barriers will be transportation. Illness. They lost permanent housing and they don’t want to say it. … The language barrier. We have families that, they work — a single mom working two jobs,” Garay said.
Whatever the problem is, the home visitors work on finding solutions with the family.
“This is about a change in mindset. It’s moving from blame to engagement and prevention,” said Attendance Works CEO Hedy Chang, who has worked with Connecticut on LEAP since the program’s inception.
According to Ajit Gopalakrishnan of the Connecticut State Department of Education, students served through LEAP improve their rate of attendance by double digits on average and receive fewer disciplinary actions. A 2023 brief from Attendance Works reported a number of other qualitative benefits for families, including a better awareness of resources and a deeper sense of belonging and accountability.
In 2021, the program served 15 high-need districts; today, it serves 25, with plans to expand further in the near future. A $7 million line item for LEAP in the state budget has replaced the now-expired ARPA funding.
Chang attributed LEAP’s success to how Connecticut collects attendance data: Years before the pandemic, Connecticut began insisting schools report attendance data monthly, rather than yearly. The state also developed a clear definition of what “attendance” actually is, including for virtual learning.
Chang said having those structures in place when COVID hit was instrumental in making LEAP work.
“It allows you to have a much earlier warning sign that things are going awry,” Chang said.
The fact that many other states don’t collect the amount of data Connecticut does — and that “chronic absence” may not even mean exactly the same thing from one state to another — makes it hard to compare the Nutmeg State’s performance to the nation as a whole (in Connecticut, chronic absenteeism is defined as missing 10% of school days in a school year). Nevertheless, Chang said, Connecticut compares well to many of its peers.
She offered a few theories about why chronic absenteeism remains above pre-pandemic levels. First: Attitudes toward being school haven’t yet gone back to what they were before COVID.
“There have been challenges coming back from the pandemic of kids and families fully appreciating that being in school in person matters,” Chang said.
She said the challenges low-income households have faced after COVID, such as rising food prices and housing insecurity, have also made school attendance worse. Many federal health, housing and nutrition programs have also received substantial cuts since the passage of 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
And then there’s ICE.
“There is research … that shows that when you have ICE raids at or near schools, it — particularly for those days, it affects (attendance),” Chang said. And that doesn’t just go for undocumented students; Chang said students with legal residence are also wary of going to school when ICE is in the neighborhood.
Nevertheless, Education Commissioner Charlene Russell-Tucker said Connecticut is aiming to bring its chronic absence numbers down even further. The State Board of Education has set a target of 6% chronic absenteeism statewide; Russell-Tucker described that number as ambitious but achievable.
“It’s bold … but I really believe that it just causes us to dig in even more,” Russell-Tucker said.
As for Lamont, his message to students at the start of the school year was simple: “Come to school. We miss you. We love you.”

Third Army Corps outlines recruitment model under conditional early discharge procedure
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
18:51:11 EEST
00:51:11 KST

The Third Army Corps provided details on the specifics of its recruitment model under the conditional early discharge procedure: applications from interested individuals come from many sources, but a personal interview conducted according to a clear protocol is mandatory.
When asked how the selection process works for inmates who have expressed a desire to serve in the military, comrade Manhust said applications from interested individuals come from many sources, including the Ukrainian Army Recruitment Center and hotlines.
"That is, they receive calls from correctional facilities, and those who express a desire to join, for example, the Third Separate Mechanized Brigade – that’s where it comes down to us, to me. Convicts themselves also have the option to use paid IP telephony, and recruitment posters are displayed throughout the facilities – so they see the number, call, sign up, and ask to join. And, of course, word of mouth still works: someone has already been released, someone is already fighting in our ranks and passes on the ‘news’ to correctional facilities that ‘guys, it’s great here, people treat you like a human being here,’ and others start signing up," the soldier said.
The head of the conditional early discharge of the recruitment division added that the Third Army Corps has its own teams of recruiters who travel throughout Ukraine, visiting all correctional facilities.
"We "cover" absolutely every correctional facility. So when we receive a request, the guys compile a list of these people, visit the facility, and invite them for an interview. We always conduct in-person interviews – we do not grant written consent remotely," Manhust said.
According to him, the interview process follows a standardized procedure: there is a clearly defined structure, specific questions are asked, a psychological profile of the individual is established, and their suitability is assessed, among other things. In addition, medical professionals are always present on the recruitment teams, and they are required to conduct an initial medical examination before the candidate undergoes the Medical Examination Commission.
"In other words, even though a convicted person who has enlisted in the Armed Forces of Ukraine will still be required to undergo a medical board examination, our medical professionals first examine the person, ask questions, and conduct a rapid test for viral diseases," the military official said.
He noted that only after this is a written consent form issued to the person wishing to join the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
"We then guide the individual through the medical examination process, prepare their military registration documents, submit the materials to the court that approves the conscription, and we accept them into our ranks," Manhust said.
However, according to him, there are certain legal restrictions on the possibility of enlisting a convict into the army.
"That is, there are restrictions based on specific criminal charges: for example, sex crimes and intentional homicide. Regarding the latter, there are certain provisions that the law prohibits – accordingly, we do not consider such individuals," the Third Army Corps said.
In addition, Manhust said the corps has additional internal rules: a strict ban on drug addicts. Also, according to the Special Forces Directorate, only men can be recruited into the Third Army Corps.
Speaking about age restrictions, Manhust said that since the service involves field operations and involves infantry units, physical condition, health, and age are very important.
"Actually, if a person is over 40, we tend to be more selective. They may feel physically well and strong, but when they put on all their combat gear, under physical strain, carrying heavy loads, and under stress, chronic conditions, for example, tend to surface," the head of the recruitment division said.
However, if a person has already turned 18, they can join the Special Forces, Manhust added.
"The only caveat is that in some cases, the law stipulates that consent from a parent is required until the person turns 21. In other words, the parents must submit a written statement indicating that they have no objections and permit their child to sign a contract with the Armed Forces of Ukraine," the corps said.

'World looking at India as bright spot of growth & hope': PM Modi at Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 21, 2026, 21:20 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small

Large
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday said the world is looking at India as a "bright spot of growth and hope", stressing that the country's reform journey has shifted from a "punishment model" under the earlier licence raj governments to an incentive-based approach.Addressing the Economic Times World Leaders Forum 2026, PM Modi said the world had witnessed several ups and downs in recent years and that the future of all nations was interconnected.
"The world has witnessed many ups and downs over the past few years, and these experiences have made one thing abundantly clear: whether one likes it or not, the futures of all nations are interconnected. Nothing is possible in isolation," the Prime Minister said."'One Earth, One Family, One Future' was India's guiding mantra during its G20 presidency. This spirit of a shared future, along with the accompanying sense of responsibility, offers solutions to many of the challenges facing the 21st-century world. There are various concerns regarding global growth. The world has witnessed a grim scenario recently; resources are being weaponized, and an atmosphere of mistrust is giving rise to numerous new challenges.
Yet, even in such times, the world views India as a bright spot of growth and hope," he added.
From 'production-linked punishment' to PLI
PM Modi criticised the earlier licence raj governments, saying they followed a "Production Linked Punishment" (PLP) model that penalised companies for increasing production.“Today’s younger generation will be surprised to hear that there was a time in our country when if a company produced more than the prescribed limit, it was punished. This was the PLP, or Production Linked Punishment, model of the earlier licence raj governments,” he said.“Those who make fun of the Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat campaigns today are rooted in the same thinking of the past — PLP, or Production Linked Punishment,” he said.
'Prohibited unless permitted' to 'permitted unless prohibited'
PM Modi also said the government is changing the country's regulatory philosophy by moving away from the earlier approach of requiring permission for activities unless explicitly allowed.“Earlier, the approach to regulations was ‘prohibited unless permitted’ — meaning you could not do something unless the government gave you permission. We are changing this approach to ‘permitted unless prohibited’. That means, for anything that is not explicitly prohibited by law, there should be no need to seek permission at every step.”He said the shift was intended to recast the relationship between the state, citizens and businesses around trust rather than suspicion.“The relationship between the government and citizens should be based not on suspicion, but on trust,” PM Modi added.The Prime Minister also highlighted legislative work undertaken during the Monsoon Session of Parliament."In the Monsoon Session of Parliament, we have passed the Bankers’ Books Evidence Bill, even as the Opposition has continued to create disruptions in Parliament. We did not allow the work of serving the country to stop," he said."We are not just changing regulations, we are changing entire policy of regulations," PM Modi said at the ET Global Leaders' Forum.Speaking ahead of PM Modi's keynote address at the summit, Times Internet chairman Satyan Gajwani said Modi had emerged as a source of stability in a world "lurching from one crisis to the next."
Gajwani said the global landscape was being reshaped by multiple, overlapping disruptions - two ongoing wars, an energy crisis, disrupted shipping routes, trade wars and the rapid AI revolution - creating unprecedented uncertainty for governments, businesses and economies.He said India's political and economic stability, coupled with its growth and reform trajectory, had positioned the country as a reliable force amid growing geopolitical uncertainty.Gajwani said PM Modi's leadership and policy continuity had helped provide businesses and investors with greater predictability, while giving India an opportunity to play a larger role in the evolving global order.

At least 3 injured in sword attack at Swedish high school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:47:00 UTC
00:47:00 KST

One person was killed, at least three others were injured after an 18-year-old armed with a sword targeted a high school in central Sweden on Friday before police shot and detained him, authorities said, as reports emerged that the suspect was a former student with a previous assault conviction.
The attack unfolded Friday afternoon at Brinell High School in Fagersta, a town of about 13,000 people. The school had just reopened after the summer break, and for some students, it was their first day back.
Police said at a news conference that officers responding to the school shot and subdued the 18-year-old suspect before taking him into custody on suspicion of murder.
Local police chief Tommy Alriksson said officers entered the school shortly after arriving at the scene.
"The first patrol entered and let us know that the perpetrator was subdued with gunfire," Alriksson said.
Swedish public broadcaster SVT, citing unnamed sources, reported that the attacker was wearing a helmet and carrying a sword. It said he was a former student at the school and had previously been convicted of assault.
Local health authorities said two of those wounded were teenage boys who suffered severe injuries. A third injured person was released from the hospital.
The violence triggered a major emergency response and a five-hour lockdown at the school, which has about 450 students between the ages of 16 and 20. Several other schools and public buildings in Fagersta were also initially placed under lockdown.
One student, Nellie, said the school day had begun normally before she saw an injured person covered in blood and police officers rushing into the building.
Another student, Abdulrahem Salmo, told SVT he saw a victim with a bloody wound to the arm before students fled and contacted police.
Fagersta Mayor Asa-Marta Sjostrom said the attack had shaken the small community and that authorities were focused on supporting students, school employees and others affected by the violence.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson canceled a speech scheduled for Saturday following the attack, according to Swedish news agency TT.
"Our thoughts are with all those affected," Kristersson said on X.
King Carl XVI Gustaf said in a statement released by the royal household that he received news of the attack "with dismay and sadness."
Social Democratic Party leader Magdalena Andersson, whose center-left coalition leads opinion polls ahead of next month's parliamentary election, expressed solidarity with the community.
"All of Sweden stands together with Fagersta at this difficult time," she said.
Police were also investigating a TikTok account potentially linked to the attack, according to Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet. The account reportedly posted an image of a sword about 20 minutes before the violence began.
Dagens Nyheter reported that details visible in the background suggested the image may have been taken inside a restroom at the school.
Before the month-old account was removed Friday, it contained videos referring to two previous episodes of mass violence in Sweden as well as Norwegian far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik.
The attack comes amid memories of previous deadly violence at Swedish schools. In February 2025, a gunman killed 10 people at a school in Orebro before killing himself in Sweden's deadliest mass shooting.
In 2015, a masked attacker armed with a sword killed a teaching assistant and two students at a school in Trollhattan in western Sweden before police shot him dead. Authorities later determined that the attack was racially motivated.

Peleg Design brings a little reptilian assistance to windy beach days with Crococlips, a set of crocodile-shaped grips designed to keep towels securely in place. Attached to the corners of a towel, the compact accessories clamp onto the fabric and help prevent it from folding, shifting or taking an unscheduled trip across the sand when the wind picks up.
The idea follows the studio’s familiar formula of combining function with visual humor. Rather than disguising the mechanism, Crococlips turn the gripping action itself into the joke: the crocodile’s open jaws close around the textile, transforming a straightforward fastening device into a characterful beach companion. One on each corner, and the towel suddenly has its own small security team.
the crocodile-shaped clips secure towels in place | images courtesy of Peleg Design
A BITE-SIZED SOLUTION TO WINDY DAYS
Designed for beaches, picnics and other outdoor settings, the clips respond to an everyday inconvenience with an intentionally simple gesture. Their pronounced jaws create a secure hold on the fabric, while the animal silhouette makes their purpose immediately legible. Instead of adding another technical-looking accessory to the beach bag, Peleg Design gives the mechanism a personality of its own.
That approach reflects the broader philosophy of the studio, founded by Shahar Peleg in 2004. Peleg Design develops household and lifestyle objects around three recurring principles — functionality, aesthetics and humor — often using visual twists and playful associations to rethink familiar products. Crococlips continue this strategy at a particularly modest scale: no reinvention of the beach towel required, just something determined enough to hold onto it.
each clip grips onto the edge of the fabric
FUNCTION GETS A SENSE OF HUMOR
The clips also embody Peleg Design’s interest in objects that reveal their idea almost instantly. Their crocodile form is not merely decorative but tied directly to the way the product works, with the metaphorical bite becoming a literal gripping mechanism. This overlap between image and function allows an otherwise ordinary accessory to operate somewhere between practical tool and small visual gag.
For a product designed to solve such a minor problem, Crococlips make a surprisingly visible intervention. They keep fabric anchored while adding a playful detail to the edges of a towel or blanket, turning wind resistance into something a little less serious. The beach may remain unpredictable, but at least the crocodiles are holding on.

US Destroys Its Own MQ-9 Reaper Drone After Emergency Landing in Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:45:46 UTC
00:45:46 KST

The U.S. MQ-9A Reaper drone crashed in the Middle East due to a fuel system malfunction. After the drone made an emergency landing in an undisclosed country, U.S. military personnel destroyed the wreckage to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands.
According to a report by the U.S. Air Force aviation mishap investigation board, the incident was caused by damaged wiring in the fuel system, which led to a short circuit and shut down the engine. The crew, operating the drone from Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota, made two unsuccessful attempts to restart the engine while the aircraft was still airborne.
The pilot glided the unmanned aircraft with its engine inoperative for nearly 10 minutes before making a forced landing, during which the landing gear collapsed. The incident occurred while the drone was carrying out a 19-hour mission in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility.
Because recovering the drone from the landing site was not possible, U.S. special operations forces removed its most sensitive equipment and then destroyed the aircraft in place.
The report states that the incident occurred during the aircraft’s first flight following scheduled maintenance and an engine replacement carried out by civilian contractors from Amentum. However, the investigation board, led by Colonel Brian Desautels, concluded that the maintenance personnel’s engine replacement was not the cause of the wiring damage.
The U.S. Air Force has lost approximately one-quarter of its entire MQ-9 Reaper fleet as a result of the war with Iran.

lotus-shaped bamboo roof floats over pablo luna studio’s yoga space in bali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:45:13 UTC
00:45:13 KST

Pablo Luna Studio completes a bamboo pavilion for yoga in Bali whose roof spreads outward to recall a lotus when seen from above. The reference is literal enough to read from the air, while the building feels looser from the ground, where the petal edges extend beyond a circular floor deck and a sparse ring of bamboo supports. Set on a planted slope beside a river, the shala sits slightly above the terrain, with the forest continuing right up to its edge.
The architects began developing Lotus Yoga Shala in 2021 and describes it as one of the first buildings through which the practice explored biomimicry. The broad lotus silhouette was maintained throughout the long development stage, but in its finished form much of the building’s character comes from the dense bamboo work underneath.
Each of Pablo Luna Studio’s ‘lotus petals’ grows from a structural system of petung bamboo that turns the floral outline into the actual construction of the roof. Its primary arches bundle three lengths of petung, while split bamboo forms an interwoven gridshell across them. At the perimeter, loads gather into clusters of three to five bamboo poles. The supports concentrate around these structural junctions, leaving broad openings between them and keeping the edge of the pavilion visually open toward the landscape.
From inside, the roof becomes a dense drawing of crossing bamboo ribs, with woven panels stretched between them to filter daylight. The construction has enough pattern to give the ceiling its own visual weight, even as the floor plate stays simple beneath it. Hoping to preserve the existing contours and limiting contact with the ground, the architects design the raised platform to follow the hillside instead of flattening it.
Pablo Luna Studio shapes a bamboo roof as an array of overlapping lotus petals
the landscape stays inside the room
Conventional walls largely disappear around the practice space, which leaves the roof overhead as its strongest spatial boundary. Views extend toward the river and dense vegetation, while daylight and air move freely through the perimeter. For a pavilion intended for yoga and meditation, that openness gives the building much of its atmosphere before any wellness language enters the picture. The floor and canopy simply frame the surrounding landscape as part of the room.
The lotus gives the shala an easy visual identity, though the more convincing move is how Pablo Luna Studio makes that image structural. The petal outline grows directly from the roof system, and the same curved geometry creates broad shelter with relatively few columns. At 125 square meters, the building remains compact, with most of its presence coming from a canopy that expands far beyond the deck and seems to hover among the vegetation. It is a small pavilion whose roof largely defines its identity.
the 125 square-meter pavilion open outward over the river and forest
arched petung bamboo members form the primary structure beneath the canopy
a split bamboo gridshell ties the curved roof into a continuous shell
clusters of bamboo columns leave broad openings around the perimeter
the elevated floor follows the existing contours of the hillside
woven bamboo filters daylight across the practice space
Opposite Office has opened a new office - in a tree. One square metre, two to three architects, and no rent. The Baumhaus Office is a radical experiment in how little an architecture practice actually needs.

‘Islands of biodiversity’ offer hope for recovery after High Fens fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:43:10 UTC
00:43:10 KST

Amid the charred plains of the High Fens, small areas have been largely spared by the fire that has ravaged the nature reserve over the past week. Conservationists have been able to confirm this now that the situation on the ground is under control. These “islands of biodiversity” are important for recovery in the coming years.
‘Islands of biodiversity’ offer hope for recovery after High Fens fire
Over the past week, 3,000 hectares of the High Fens in Liège province have been reduced to ashes by the fire that began on Friday. The impact is enormous, but not everything has been destroyed.
Small pockets of nature have been spared in the affected area. These form when the wind suddenly drives the fire in a different direction. The exact extent of the ecological damage will become clear in the coming weeks and months.
“Based on visual footage alone, it is difficult to form a clear picture of what the real impact is,” says Kris Verheyen, professor of forest ecology and forest management at Ghent University. “One of the things that is difficult to see is how much of the peat has actually been burnt or damaged.”
It is already clear, however, that the affected area is not a uniform whole. Some zones have been severely affected, others less so. The ground is still smouldering in various places, meaning the situation continues to evolve.
Based on visual footage alone, it is difficult to form a clear picture of what the real impact is
According to Verheyen, the fact that some areas have survived could play a key role in the area’s recovery. “If populations of certain species are still present in those areas, then the recolonisation of the burnt areas will be a lot easier,” he says. This applies not only to animals but also to rare plant species.
An iconic species of the High Fens is the extremely rare black grouse. It is doubtful whether that population survived the fire, but a male was found alive by the fire brigade on Thursday.
The exact impact on the fauna and flora will only become clear after extensive field research. Drones and aerial photographs will be used to map the site in detail.
The fact that the area has been severely affected does not mean it will remain black for years. “It will probably turn green again relatively quickly,” says Verheyen. “But that greenery will mainly be dominated by purple moor grass.”
This is a type of grass that is common in heathland and peatland areas and even benefits from large wildfires to spread further. As it is highly flammable, it increases the risk of fire during dry periods.
However, controlling the plant – for example, through grazing – is difficult in such a vast and inaccessible reserve.
“Anyone going for a walk in the High Fens in a few years’ time will, apart from the burnt trees, not notice much of the fire at first glance,” Verheyen says. “If you look more closely at the rarer species and at the peat itself, you will continue to see the traces for a very long time.”

FIFA suspends Argentina players, fines football association over World Cup incidents

Dilara Hamit
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
FIFA on Friday fined the Argentine Football Association (AFA) and suspended three of its players and one team official over incidents during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, including a post-match scuffle after the final against Spain.
Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes received the heaviest punishment, with FIFA's Disciplinary Committee handing him a 10-match suspension and a fine of $90,000.
Defender Nahuel Molina was suspended for seven matches and fined the same amount, while midfielder Thiago Almada received a one-match ban and a $30,000 fine.
Argentina team official Roberto Ayala was also suspended for three matches and fined $30,000.
Spain midfielder Gavi received a one-match suspension and a $30,000 fine over his involvement in the incident.
The sanctions followed a confrontation after Spain defeated Argentina in the World Cup final in the US last month.
FIFA also fined the AFA $321,000 over several disciplinary violations during the tournament, including the display of a banner relating to the disputed Falkland Islands, known as the Malvinas in Argentina, following the semifinal against England.
Of the fine, $100,000 must be invested in an anti-discrimination plan, while another $100,000 has been suspended subject to a probationary period.
Argentina was also ordered to play their next two home matches with stadium capacity limited to 50%.
FIFA said the sanctions related to breaches including “using a sports event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature,” discrimination, misconduct and breaches of security regulations.
The governing body said the decisions followed disciplinary proceedings over incidents during the World Cup and were subject to appeal where applicable.

The Hidden Famine: What I Saw in North Korea’s Darkest Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:40:00 UTC
00:40:00 KST

“Miss Kathi: Saving Lives in North Korea” by Kathi Zellweger and Mike Chinoy chronicles the remarkable story of Kathi Zellweger, a native of Switzerland whose history of engagement with a secretive, isolated North Korea over nearly three decades is unprecedented in its scope, access, and humanitarian impact. It is one of the first book-length accounts in English by an aid worker operating on the ground in North Korea – the story of a woman who has lived out her commitment to the poor and most vulnerable undaunted by the tensions and threat of conflict perpetually looming over the Korean peninsula.
For many North Koreans, Kathi was the first foreigner they had ever met or even seen. Playing a central role in the early years of international relief efforts in North Korea was a lonely job, as Kathi addressed the humanitarian needs of a suffering people largely ignored by the world because of their citizenship. She befriended local doctors, nurses, and caregivers; negotiated with suspicious government officials; overcame international doubts about the diversion of relief supplies to the military; and, over a period of years, spearheaded an effort that provided food, medicine, and development aid. Ultimately, her efforts saved the lives of thousands of people – most of them children.
This excerpt from the book describes visits to people struggling to survive the famine in the northern city of Sinuiju.
It was September 1998. I sat on the floor, Korean style, in Mrs. Kim’s apartment in Sinuiju, one of North Korea’s five largest cities. Located on the banks of the Yalu River just across from the Chinese town of Dandong, Sinuiju had been an important industrial center and a key transit point for trade with China before North Korea’s economy collapsed. Yet even though there was more contact with China in Sinuiju now than in other North Korean cities, it remained shabby and dilapidated, especially in contrast to the bright lights and bustling streets visible on the Chinese side of the Yalu in Dandong.
And Sinuiju had not been immune to the devastating impact of the famine. Indeed, earlier in the year, the North Koreans and the World Food Program had asked Caritas, the international charity where I worked, to ship 1,500 metric tons of barley there. As was often the case, providing the aid opened the door for me to visit an area that had previously been off limits to visitors. Along with Mary Healy, a nurse and midwife from the Irish NGO Trócaire (Caritas Ireland), which had become one of our most important international partners, I was making my first trip there. Local officials told us that, for many people, our supplies had been crucial in keeping hunger at bay. But the situation remained bleak.
At the Amnokgang Hotel, a large, square building with damp, smelly rooms and balconies whose doors could not be opened, we were virtually the only guests in the cavernous dining hall. The hotel shop offered an eclectic collection of basic necessities, but most striking to me was the jewelry that was also on sale. It was evident that some desperate citizens had pawned their personal valuables to get money to buy food. I bought a pair of earrings inlaid with small red stones. I still have them today. I keep them in a box. They bring back sad memories.
In a dismal gray Stalinist-style building typical of most North Korean cities, 69-year-old Mrs. Kim shared a tiny flat with her son, daughter-in-law, and six-month-old grandson. The son and his wife both worked in a nearby textile factory. Mrs. Kim and her daughter-in-law kept the apartment spotless. On one wall hung a guitar, which Mrs. Kim’s son apparently liked to play.
As I entered the room, I was startled to hear the gravel-tinged vocals of American country music legend Kenny Rogers coming from a cassette recorder. It made for an incongruous juxtaposition with the obligatory pictures of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il mounted on another wall. I was tempted to ask about the music, but it occurred to me that the tape and the cassette player likely had come from China, that Mrs. Kim might well not be aware that Rogers was an American, and that the “guardian angels” accompanying us were probably equally ignorant. Inquiring as to why the family had popular music from the United States could have caused trouble for everyone, so I stayed silent. Mary and I just looked at each other with slightly puzzled expressions.
Under other circumstances, owning items such as a guitar and a cassette recorder, or the sewing machines and refrigerators I saw in other urban homes, would, in North Korean terms, have been signs of a decent standard of living. But on this visit, they could not mask the family’s grim plight.
“Is this the end of the Great Leader taking care of us?” the daughter-in-law asked plaintively. Her baby was ill. She said she was still breastfeeding and planned to continue to do so as long as possible. She had nothing else to feed her son. Six months had passed since they had received their last rations through the Public Distribution System. Apart from 14 kilos of rice and some bean curd delivered to mark North Korea’s National Day, they had been subsisting on alternative food plus whatever they could obtain by bartering textiles and other items with relatives who lived in the countryside and were able to grow some food for themselves.
Later that day, Mary and I were taken to meet the family of Mr. Lee, a 71-year-old carpenter. We found him sitting on his living room floor designing some furniture. He was surprised to see two unexpected foreign visitors but was gracious and friendly. Mr. Lee lived with his wife and youngest son. Three older sons were married and lived elsewhere. Like Mrs. Kim, Mr. Lee told us he had last received rations from the Public Distribution System in February. He was surviving by making furniture for people in the countryside, which he exchanged for food.
The examples of the Kim and Lee families highlighted two important characteristics of the famine in North Korea. Its epicenter was in urban rather than rural areas. More than two-thirds of the population lived in or near cities and towns. Unlike farmers in the countryside, who had the ability to grow some food on small private plots, which the authorities understood were necessary to survive and thus (perhaps grudgingly) tolerated, urban residents, often stuck in large apartment blocks, had no such option.
The result was unprecedented hunger in what had been a relatively well developed modern industrial society. With the collapse of the Public Distribution System, which had been the sole source of food, many urban residents, unable to grow anything for themselves, simply wasted away in their homes, starving quietly and out of sight. This was one reason I began to describe the situation as a “hidden famine.” In contrast to predominantly rural Somalia or Ethiopia, the worst suffering was not immediately visible. That didn’t make it any less real.
For the families we visited in Sinuiju, and many others, bartering was a crucial survival mechanism. What had begun with urban residents trading items of value, either from their homes or what could be stripped from their places of work, for food grown by farmers in private family garden plots became the foundation for the broader development of markets. As I traveled around the country, I would see people by the side of the road selling everything from buns to cigarettes to vegetables to live fish. As time passed, I also started to see little businesses appearing – people mending shoes, sewing, fixing bicycle tires, transporting wood in simple carts. Almost all of those involved appeared to be women, presumably because men were more likely to have fixed jobs or be serving in the military.
The emergence of these markets was a sensitive political issue. As a de facto privatization of an important part of North Korea’s economy, they posed not only practical challenges to state control but also an ideological one. Initially, when roadside vendors noticed a foreigner like me approaching, they would quickly cover the plastic buckets containing their products and run away. The government officials accompanying me were visibly uncomfortable as well and would often look in the other direction.
But the trend only accelerated with the creation of larger markets, especially in or near urban areas, which took over the role of the largely nonfunctional Public Distribution System. Before long, they became not only a source of food but of many other goods, although as they expanded, prices rose as well, and many people remained too poor or too far away to benefit. Indeed, some people told us they were spending up to 80 percent of their salary just to purchase vegetables.
The availability of cereals was a particularly sensitive issue. The government jealously guarded its monopoly on distributing items such as rice and maize. Occasionally, these products did make their way to the markets but were usually hidden from the public and sold surreptitiously.
In 2002, in an effort to reform the economy, in conjunction with a broader outreach to Tokyo, Washington, and Europe, Kim Jong Il formally sanctioned the existence of some markets in cities and towns. Before then, however, they operated in a kind of gray area. At that time, foreigners were forbidden from visiting them, which made it hard to determine the precise nature, scale, and impact of the phenomenon, but sometimes on my colleagues’ and my travels, we would end up driving right through one, with crowds of people stepping aside to let our vehicle pass. It was yet another of the many paradoxes of North Korea.
Excerpted from “Miss Kathi: Saving Lives in North Korea”
By Kathi Zellweger and Mike Chinoy © 2026 by Kathi Zellweger and Mike Chinoy

Egypt asylum shift deepens 'Fortress Europe' concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:39:45 UTC
00:39:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt asylum shift deepens 'Fortress Europe' concerns
Egypt began implementing a new state-run asylum system on Friday, as rights groups warned that the move could deepen the EU's reliance on Cairo to keep refugees and migrants away from Europe's borders despite documented abuses.
Executive regulations for Egypt's 2024 asylum law came into force on 21 August, beginning a transition that will transfer responsibility for registering asylum seekers and determining refugee status from the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) to a government committee under the authority of the prime minister.
The change comes as the EU increasingly relies on Egypt as a key partner in efforts to reduce irregular migration.
his is part of a broader policy of shifting border management beyond Europe's territory that critics have dubbed "Fortress Europe".
Under a strategic partnership agreed in 2024, the EU pledged a €7.4 billion financial package to Egypt up to 2027, including €200 million specifically for migration and mobility.
The funding covers border management, efforts against smuggling and trafficking, returns and reintegration.
Robert Springborg, an expert on Egyptian politics and adjunct professor at Simon Fraser University, told The New Arab that migration control had become central to Cairo's relationship with Brussels.
"No other issue is more important in this bilateral relationship," he said, arguing that European financial support rewards Egypt for "managing" - or preventing - irregular migration from Egypt and neighbouring countries.
Rights groups have repeatedly warned, however, that European migration cooperation with Egypt risks supporting an increasingly securitised system in which refugees and migrants have faced arbitrary arrest, detention, torture, sexual violence and deportation.
Springborg said Egypt had "embarked on a security-first approach both because it is being rewarded by Europe for so doing, and because it perceives the presence of a large number of refugees as posing security threats".
Amnesty International documented in 2024 how Egyptian Border Guard Forces, whose capabilities had been supported under an earlier €80 million EU programme, carried out mass arrests of Sudanese refugees and forcibly returned hundreds to Sudan without allowing them to seek asylum or challenge their removal.
Michelle Randhawa, senior refugee and migrant rights officer at Human Rights Watch, said European support for Egypt's migration policies raised serious concerns.
"One of the EU's core values is respect for human rights, so to finance migration control in Egypt while ignoring the violations of human rights of refugees and asylum seekers is deeply troubling to say the least," she told The New Arab.
"The EU should not be strengthening the capacity of the Egyptian government to detain and deport refugees and asylum seekers while failing to ensure that they can access protection and are not returned to serious harm."
Crackdown on refugees
Those concerns have persisted as Egypt has expanded its crackdown on refugees and asylum seekers.
In February, Amnesty documented the arrests of 22 refugees and asylum seekers, including a child and two women, between late December 2025 and early February. Fifteen were registered with UNHCR.
Human Rights Watch reported in July that refugees and asylum seekers, primarily from Sudan and South Sudan, had been subjected to months of arbitrary arrest, detention and deportation, including people with valid UNHCR cards.
Some were being given appointments as late as 2028 to renew residency documents because of government backlogs, HRW said, while remaining vulnerable to arrest for failing to possess valid permits.
Randhawa said the administrative backlog was itself creating risks for refugees.
"We found that many refugees and asylum seekers are being arrested and, in some cases, deported simply because the government's bureaucratic backlog of residency renewals is forcing them into a situation where their residency expires while waiting for a renewal date," she said.
"Without addressing this backlog, the new system risks effectively making this administrative failure into a protection failure."
The organisation also documented overcrowded detention facilities, inadequate access to food and clean water, physical abuse and racial profiling of sub-Saharan African refugees.
Egyptian authorities do not publish comprehensive figures for refugee arrests or deportations. Egyptian rights organisations cited by Amnesty estimated that between 3,000 and 5,000 refugees and asylum seekers were deported in January and February alone.
More than 1.1 million people were registered with UNHCR in Egypt as of the end of May, up around 275 percent from before the outbreak of Sudan's war in April 2023.
Around 852,000 were Sudanese, whose registered population in Egypt has increased by more than 1,300 percent since the war began. Syrians were the second-largest group, with around 98,000 registered.
The scale of Sudanese displacement has become central to Cairo's argument that Egypt is carrying a heavy economic and social burden requiring greater international support.
Egypt takes control of asylum
But the new asylum regime will also give the Egyptian state significantly greater control over those displaced populations.
For more than seven decades, refugee-status determination in Egypt has been handled by UNHCR under a 1954 agreement. Under the new system, a Permanent Committee for Refugee Affairs will ultimately determine who is recognised as a refugee and who can remain in the country.
The transfer will not happen immediately, with the regulations providing for a transitional period in which existing files and data are handed over and UNHCR continues to play a role.
Randhawa said there remained "a lack of transparency in how the transition will play out", including uncertainty over UNHCR's role, the asylum application backlog and information sharing.
HRW sent a follow-up letter to the Egyptian government in June asking what training would be provided to officials responsible for interviewing asylum seekers and conducting refugee-status determinations, but Randhawa said the organisation had yet to receive a response.
"The problem isn't Egypt creating and implementing an asylum framework, but that they are doing it hastily without adequate safeguards, consultations, information sharing, and before the asylum infrastructure is even functional," she said.
Refugees Platform in Egypt has nevertheless called for implementation to be suspended, warning before Friday's deadline that there remained insufficient clarity over how responsibilities would be transferred and how international protection would be maintained.
The regulations also require people who entered Egypt irregularly to apply for asylum within 45 days, while rejected applicants can face removal.
Rights organisations have raised concerns over protections against refoulement, the forcible return of people to countries where they face persecution or serious harm, and the new committee's broad powers on national security and public order.
Randhawa called it "deeply concerning" that the new law does not explicitly prohibit refoulement, warning that people facing detention or deportation could be returned to places where they face persecution or serious harm.
For critics of European migration policy, Egypt's transition illustrates a wider shift in which the EU increasingly seeks to manage migration before people reach its territory.
As Cairo assumes greater power to decide who receives protection and who does not, Europe is simultaneously investing heavily in Egypt's capacity to manage and contain migration before it reaches the Mediterranean.

Europe urged to step up mosquito controls as West Nile cases rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
15:36:40 UTC
00:36:40 KST

Aysu Biçer
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Europe must strengthen its efforts to control mosquitoes as the risk of mosquito-borne diseases increases, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) has warned.
Six European regions have reported locally acquired West Nile virus (WNV) infections for the first time this year. As of Aug. 13, 429 locally acquired cases had been recorded across nine countries.
Transmission usually peaks in August and early September, meaning further cases are expected, the ECDC said.
“The expansion of West Nile virus transmission as well as the spread of invasive mosquito species demonstrate why Europe needs to strengthen its mosquito-control capacity,” said Celine Gossner of the ECDC in a statement on Thursday.
The Asian tiger mosquito, which can spread dengue and chikungunya, is now established in 16 European countries – twice as many as 12 years ago.
An article published by the ECDC and EU partners in the Eurosurveillance journal has called for greater coordination and a wider range of mosquito-control measures.
The ECDC said effective control should combine mosquito and disease monitoring, management of stagnant water, community involvement and targeted measures suited to local conditions.
It also warned that insecticide resistance, environmental concerns and a limited number of authorized products were making mosquito control more difficult.
People can help reduce mosquito numbers by removing or covering stagnant water around homes, while repellents, protective clothing and mosquito-proofing can provide personal protection.
Healthcare professionals have also been urged to remain alert to local transmission and imported infections.
