====================================================================================================

‘The country is falling apart’: Record Israeli departures signal deeper shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:36:34 UTC
22:36:34 KST

A record wave of Israelis leaving the country is increasingly drawing attention not only for its scale, but for the profile of those departing, with research pointing to a growing outflow of highly educated, high-earning professionals.
Nearly 270,000 Israeli citizens left the country for at least three consecutive months between 2023 and 2025, according to a Tel Aviv University study released this month, marking a sharp increase from comparable levels a decade earlier.
The trend has raised warnings of a potential brain drain, with studies showing doctors, engineers, academics and other skilled professionals leaving in high numbers.
Independent Israeli political commentator and former university professor Ori Goldberg told Anadolu that the trend reflects a broader loss of stability in Israel.
"The country is falling apart. It lacks stability," Goldberg said.
He said many of those leaving expect "stability," functioning state services and guarantees that public institutions will operate at a satisfactory level, while also tending to hold relatively liberal views.
"The numbers are much larger than they usually are. The balance of people who are leaving against people who are coming is much larger than it usually is," he said.
A Tel Aviv University study based on Central Bureau of Statistics data found that 268,509 Israelis left the country for at least three consecutive months between 2023 and 2025, compared with 183,219 during the corresponding three-year period a decade earlier.
Departures totaled 86,509 in 2023, 91,499 in 2024 and 90,922 in 2025.
Because official 12-month emigration figures for 2025 will not be available until 2027, researchers used departures lasting at least three consecutive months as an early indicator. They estimated that 45,000 to 50,000 Israelis likely remained abroad for at least a year in 2025.
Separate data presented during a Knesset committee debate in June also showed a sharp deterioration in the migration balance.
Israel's migration balance for Israeli citizens was negative between 2022 and 2024, declining by approximately 140,000 people over the three years, according to statistics bureau figures cited by the Knesset.
The profile of those leaving has also shifted.
Israeli emigrants aged 25-64 in 2022 were considerably more educated than the general population: the proportion holding bachelor's degrees was 1.5 times higher, master's degrees twice as high and doctoral degrees 4.6 times higher, according to data presented to lawmakers.
In 2024 alone, 530 physicians left Israel, two-thirds of whom had studied in the country, while the number of doctors returning declined.
Research by the Israel Tax Authority cited by the Times of Israel found that emigration among affluent Israelis rose sharply in 2023 and 2024, with doctors, engineers and other highly educated professionals disproportionately represented.
The average annual income of emigrants in the year before departure rose in real terms from around 125,000 shekels ($39,000) in 2015-2019 to roughly 200,000 shekels in 2024.
Goldberg said the departure of professionals presents a "real risk," particularly as conditions in sectors such as healthcare, research and technology become more difficult.
"There is a bit of a risk of a brain drain," he said, noting that those leaving tend to be "highly educated professionals."
He pointed particularly to physicians and tech workers, saying doctors sent abroad for residencies are increasingly not returning, while tech professionals have greater flexibility to relocate.
"Practicing these professions in Israel will become more and more difficult. So people will simply leave, which is what I think is happening," he said.
Goldberg attributed much of the acceleration to developments since October 2023, when Israel launched a genocidal war on Gaza following an attack by Hamas, arguing that the security crisis and subsequent political and social changes cannot be separated.
"I think most of it is because of October 2023," he said.
"The political developments and the polarization and controversy and the social questions developed because of the collective trauma experienced since October 2023."
He said the period pushed Israeli society toward a more security-oriented outlook and reinforced political divisions already visible during the controversy over the government's judicial overhaul.
The Tel Aviv University researchers similarly noted that public concern over emigration increased after the November 2022 elections and the judicial overhaul dispute, before intensifying following October 2023.
Researchers cautioned that current emigration levels do not by themselves threaten Israel's economic resilience, but warned that a sustained rise could have long-term consequences for an economy heavily dependent on a relatively small pool of skilled workers in technology, healthcare and academia.
They also raised the possibility of a feedback effect in which continued departures encourage further emigration, making the trend increasingly difficult to reverse.
Goldberg said he does not expect the current wave to simply disappear even if immediate conditions improve.
"I don't think it's such a temporary wave, and I don't think political and security conditions can be stabilized so easily," he said. "I'm not so sure Israel can simply go back to the way it was."
Research by immigration and demography scholar Lilach Lev Ari on Israelis living in the US also suggests that prolonged residence abroad can reshape migrants' relationship with their country of origin.
Her study found that while Israeli migrants maintained structural connections with Israel through family ties, digital communication and visits, longer-term migrants could simultaneously experience growing emotional distance – a phenomenon described as "transnational dissonance."
Goldberg said the current departures could therefore form part of a broader transformation rather than a short-lived response to a single crisis.
"I am assuming that Israel is entering a longer-term demographic and economic shift," he said.

Economic Watch: What foundational figure of China's NEV industry says about its rise -- and what comes next
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
21:36:31 CST
22:36:31 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- In Wan Gang's Beijing office, three objects present a compact history of China's rise in electric vehicles (EVs).
One is a kerosene lamp, a reminder of his youth spent in rural Jilin Province, where he often read by its light. Another is the Nicolaus August Otto Award, presented to him in 2023 by German engine maker DEUTZ in recognition of his pioneering work, including contributions to electric vehicles and hydrogen technology. The prize is named after the inventor of the four-stroke engine.
The third is a transparent bottle holding a miniature scene of Christopher Columbus's voyage -- a symbol, he told Xinhua, of exploring an unfamiliar frontier.
Wan, 74, is honorary president of the China Association for Science and Technology and a former minister of science and technology. He was chief scientist of the major EV project under the National High-tech R&D Program, or the 863 Program, a national initiative launched in 1986 to advance China's capabilities in strategic high-tech fields.
In a wide-ranging interview with Xinhua, Wan looked back at why China chose the EV path and set out his views on what comes next -- from competition at home and new battery technologies to the overseas development of Chinese automakers.
The interview comes as China's auto transition reaches another milestone. New energy vehicles (NEVs) -- China's official category covering pure electric vehicles, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles and fuel-cell vehicles -- accounted for 60.4 percent of all new vehicle sales in July. NEV sales reached 9.007 million in the first seven months of 2026, up 9.6 percent year on year.
Globally, China produced nearly three-quarters of the world's electric cars in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). BloombergNEF estimated that China accounted for 63 percent of electric cars sold worldwide that year.
Wan's assessment is measured: China has reached the global forefront in NEVs, he said, but "there is still much to do."
WHY CHINA CHOSE A DIFFERENT TRACK
Wan traced China's EV strategy to three practical concerns at the turn of the century: rising dependence on imported oil as car ownership grew, worsening air pollution and the risk that Chinese manufacturers would remain dependent on foreign core technologies if they continued to follow the established internal-combustion route.
EV and hybrid technologies were still in their early stages globally, leaving more room for competition. China also chose a diversified approach rather than relying on a single technology. The 863 Program's EV project pursued pure electric, hybrid and fuel-cell vehicles in parallel, while also supporting research on batteries, motors and electronic controls.
That strategy was followed by years of research, demonstration projects, infrastructure development and market building. As purchase subsidies were gradually phased out, the industry entered fully market-oriented competition.
The economics have changed markedly. The IEA estimated that, even before government incentives, nearly 70 percent of battery-electric cars sold in China in 2025 were cheaper than their internal-combustion equivalents. China also accounted for more than 80 percent of global battery-cell production, while battery-pack prices were around 30 percent lower than in North America and 35 percent lower than in Europe.
Recent 2026 analyses pointed to several drivers behind that cost advantage. McKinsey said some Chinese companies achieve battery-pack cost advantages of 25 to 40 percent through simplified architectures, lower-cost chemistries such as LFP and component optimization. CSIS highlights how private firms and technology-focused entrants intensified competition and experimentation in manufacturing, software, battery management and autonomy.
This influence is spreading beyond China. BloombergNEF said EV demand in emerging markets, including Southeast Asia and Latin America, is growing rapidly. In Thailand, electric vehicles accounted for 27 percent of new-car sales in 2025, with Chinese brands making up 88 percent of EVs sold.
China's EV deployment is also reducing oil use. The IEA estimated that the global EV fleet displaced about 1.7 million barrels of oil demand a day in 2025, with China accounting for roughly 1 million barrels a day.
China's role in the global EV transition is therefore no longer only about production volumes. Its scale has helped expand the supply of affordable EVs and lower some of the cost barriers to electrification.
ANXIETY BEHIND "INVOLUTION-STYLE" COMPETITION
Rapid growth has also brought new challenges.
Wan pointed to anxiety as one factor behind the "involution-style" competition in China's auto industry.
The sales of all automobiles in China expanded from about 26 million units in 2021 to 34 million units in 2025, with NEVs contributing a big portion of the growth. Companies rushed toward a fast-growing market, while traditional automakers had to maintain conventional vehicle businesses and compete in NEVs at the same time. Wan noted that this anxiety sometimes escalated into irrational competition.
His prescription is practical: know the customer, focus on clearer market segments and improve after-sales service. What automakers learn from existing owners, he argued, should feed directly into the next generation of products.
The need for that shift is becoming clearer. The profit margin of China's vehicle manufacturing sector fell to 1.5 percent in the first five months of 2026. Authorities have also stepped up efforts to regulate disorderly price competition and encourage companies to compete more through quality, technology and value.
Wan also rejects the characterization that China simply has too much auto capacity. He pointed to vehicle ownership of a little over 260 cars per 1,000 people -- far below levels in major developed markets -- and to room for demand to grow at home and overseas.
More recent data provide additional context. China's NEV exports reached 2.909 million in the first seven months of 2026, up 120 percent year on year, according to official industry data. BloombergNEF expected 23.3 million passenger EVs to be sold globally in 2026, an 11 percent increase from 2025.
For an industry that serves both domestic and international markets, production numbers alone don't tell the whole story. Wan emphasized that the next phase of growth should focus on better products, clearer market positioning and stronger service rather than simply increasing volume.
GOING GLOBAL MEANS GOING LOCAL
Wan is equally direct about the next stage overseas.
Chinese automakers, he said, should establish local production bases to better navigate trade barriers and build the after-sales, marketing and training systems needed for long-term operations. He pointed out that overseas service networks remain an area where Chinese brands have room for improvement.
The direction is already visible. Trade barriers and industrial policies are pushing more Chinese automakers toward local production in overseas markets. The shift is increasingly visible in Southeast Asia, with Thailand and Indonesia among the markets building deeper local EV manufacturing capabilities.
For Wan, overseas production and service are part of the same task: Chinese automakers need to understand local customers and build stronger local capabilities rather than rely only on vehicle exports.
The technology roadmap also remains open.
Wan sees pure electric vehicles as a long-term solution but expects plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, including extended-range models, to retain a substantial role. He estimated that pure electric vehicles could eventually account for about 65 to 70 percent of the combined market for the two technologies, with plug-in hybrids taking about 30 to 35 percent.
On solid-state batteries, Wan is cautious about dramatic claims on range and charging speed. The key questions, he said, are whether difficult materials and engineering problems can be solved and whether the technology makes economic sense. He expects large-scale industrialization around 2030.
That timetable is broadly consistent with recent industry assessments. McKinsey said commercial-scale production of all-solid-state batteries is unlikely until after 2030, with manufacturing hurdles around interfaces, yields, performance, longevity and cost still to be overcome.
Wan also sees hydrogen fuel cells playing a role in commercial vehicles and intelligent connected vehicles as another important direction for the industry.
Twenty-five years after China's major EV project began, the basic question is no longer whether China can build a globally competitive EV industry.
The next challenge, as Wan described it, is to improve quality and services, foster healthier competition, advance new technologies and build stronger businesses overseas.
He summed up the role he hopes China's NEV industry will play globally in three words: collaborator, pioneer and leader. China should encourage its automakers to expand overseas while continuing to welcome international companies to invest and innovate in the Chinese market, he said.
The miniature ship in Wan's office remains a fitting symbol. China's EV industry is no longer exploring an empty field. It is navigating a larger global market -- with more opportunities still ahead. ■

Economic Watch: China's civil aviation posts steady growth on rising holiday demand

BEIJING, Aug. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's civil aviation sector maintained steady growth in July, boosted by rising holiday travel demand and favorable policy support, official data showed Friday.
The sector handled about 74.63 million passenger trips last month, up 3.9 percent year on year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC).
Specifically, domestic routes handled about 67.37 million passenger trips, up 4.1 percent year on year, while international routes saw passenger trips rise 2.3 percent to 7.26 million, the CAAC said.
Cargo and mail transport registered a slight decline in July, with the total volume edging down 0.3 percent year on year to 864,000 tonnes, the regulator said.
Echoing the broad upward trend, several major Chinese airlines have recently reported their July performance, with key indicators showing growth in capacity input, passenger turnover and average seat occupancy rates.
July is traditionally one of China's busiest travel months, as summer vacations begin for universities and schools. Additionally, lower fuel surcharges by several major airlines further boosted demand for holiday travel.
"July is a peak season for air travel, and a month-on-month decline in ex-factory jet fuel prices has helped ease cost pressure on listed airlines," said Shen Xiaofeng, chief analyst with Huatai Securities.
Alongside the recovery of its domestic aviation market, China has stepped up efforts to expand its global air transport networks since the beginning of 2026. As of the end of June, Chinese airlines operated over 1,000 scheduled international routes, with passenger flights connecting the country to 80 countries worldwide.
A landmark development occurred earlier this month with the launch of the first international route operated by China's homegrown C919 aircraft, connecting Beijing with Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia.
China has also expanded its 240-hour visa-free transit program, with Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam the latest countries to be included. The policy has helped fuel a surge in cross-border travel, with Chinese border authorities handling a record 369 million inbound and outbound trips in the first half of 2026, up 10.8 percent year on year.
Looking ahead, analysts said that the long-term outlook for China's civil aviation sector remains positive despite oil price fluctuations.
In the short term, the market should continue to monitor international oil price trends, Shen said. "But in the medium to long term, we maintain our view that the industry is gradually rebounding." ■

Ebola outbreak ‘growing faster, wider’ as DRC death toll passes 2,500: UN
Epidemic in DR Congo remains out of control amid conflict, funding shortages and attacks on health workers and facilities.
The Ebola virus continues spreading “exponentially” in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the United Nations has warned.
Sounding the alarm that the outbreak is “spreading faster and wider” than ever before, the UN’s Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis reported that more than 2,500 people have now died.

The official called for more funds to be put to work to try to control the spread, noting that the existing pool of money will run out within weeks.
Efforts to stem the epidemic since the outbreak began in May have faced several challenges.
Conflict and a lack of government control and infrastructure in the eastern DRC have disrupted the effort. Where health workers – many of whom have died after contracting the virus – and facilities are able to operate, they have come under attack by frustrated and frightened locals, Harneis said.
More than 260 attacks on health workers have been reported in the past six months, and eight health workers have been killed. More than 160 healthcare workers have fallen ill, with 43 dying.
Aid workers have said many locals believe conspiracy theories that the outbreak is a hoax, and have reacted angrily when health restrictions prevent them from personally burying loved ones.
Efforts to control the outbreak have also been complicated by the lack of a vaccine for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which causes severe haemorrhagic fever.
Existing security concerns are also hampering the battle to stop the spread.
“All of this is happening in an area that has had three decades of conflict and is generating huge humanitarian needs,” Harneis said.
The UN official warned the epidemic could spread to neighbouring countries without a ramped-up response, and urged more staffing and resources to reach remote areas.

EXPLAINER – Megxit reversed? What we know about Harry and Meghan’s UK return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:30:24 UTC
22:30:24 KST

Six years after stepping away from their roles as senior working members of Britain’s royal family and starting a new life in California, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are preparing for a remarkable change of direction: a return to the UK with their two children.
The move does not signal a return to royal duties, but it marks a significant reversal for a couple whose departure was followed by explosive interviews, a Netflix documentary, Harry’s tell-all memoir and years of legal and personal battles with the royal establishment.
Their planned return also comes amid signs of a possible thaw in relations with the royal family, including a recent reunion with King Charles.
The rupture began on Jan. 8, 2020, when the Duke and Duchess of Sussex announced their intention to step back as “senior members” of the British royal family.
The announcement followed reports that the couple would relinquish their royal roles and move to Canada, claims Buckingham Palace declined to address at the time.
After spending several months in Canada before moving to the US, Harry and Meghan bought a home in Montecito, California, in June 2020.
Buckingham Palace confirmed in February 2021 that they would not return as working members of the royal family.
In March 2021, a year after their departure, CBS aired Oprah with Meghan and Harry, an interview in which the couple made some of their most serious allegations against the royal family.
Meghan accused the institution of failing to protect her and said she experienced suicidal thoughts while pregnant with Archie. She also alleged that there had been discussions within the royal family about her unborn child’s skin color.
“In those months when I was pregnant ... we have in tandem the conversation of, you won’t be given security, not going to be given a title and also concerns and conversations about how dark his skin might be when he’s born,” she said.
Meghan declined to identify the person involved, saying “that would be very damaging to them.”
“I just didn’t want to be alive anymore. And that was a very clear and real and frightening constant thought,” she said, adding that she sought help from within the institution but was denied it.
Harry, meanwhile, described the intense scrutiny the couple faced and the circumstances surrounding their exit.
Buckingham Palace later said on behalf of Queen Elizabeth II that the issues raised, particularly those involving race, would be addressed privately. Prince William subsequently rejected the allegations of racism.
The couple gave a more detailed account of their relationship and departure in the six-part Netflix documentary Harry & Meghan, released in 2022.
The series became the UK’s most-watched Netflix premiere of 2022 and recorded 81.6 million viewing hours worldwide in its first four days, the platform’s biggest debut for a documentary at the time.
In the series, Harry said: “My job is to keep my family safe. But the nature of being born into this position ... and the level of hate that is being stirred up in the last three years especially against my wife and my son, I’m generally concerned for the safety of my family.”
He said it was his “duty to uncover this exploitation and bribery that happens within our media.”
Meghan said she believed that “no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they (the media) were still going to find a way to destroy me.”
Further revelations followed in January 2023 with the publication of Harry’s memoir, Spare, which offered a deeply personal account of his deteriorating relationships with senior members of the royal family.
In the more than 550-page book, Harry described a 2019 confrontation in which William allegedly called Meghan “difficult,” “rude” and “abrasive,” language Harry characterized as a “parrot(ing of) the press narrative” about his wife.
Harry also alleged that William “knocked me to the floor” during the confrontation.
He recounted learning of Queen Elizabeth’s death while traveling to Balmoral and said Charles had told him Meghan should not accompany him.
Harry said his father phoned him: “He told me I was welcome at Balmoral, but … without her. He started to explain his reasons, but they didn’t make any sense at all, and it was disrespectful as well. I did not tolerate it from him.”
The couple’s planned return has revived questions about their publicly funded protection in Britain, which was downgraded after they stopped serving as working royals in 2020.
Harry and Meghan pay for private protection in the US. Their return, however, could require the Royal and VIP Executive Committee (RAVEC), an independent body overseen by the Home Office, to reconsider arrangements that were based on the couple being only occasional visitors to Britain, according to the BBC.
RAVEC had maintained that Harry’s security needs should be assessed on a case-by-case basis. He lost a legal challenge last year over the level of protection provided to him and his family while visiting the UK.
As neither Harry nor Meghan is expected to resume royal duties, they may not regain the level of security they had before their departure.
Asked about the issue Wednesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the couple’s security arrangements as a “private matter.”
Harry and Meghan attended Queen Elizabeth’s funeral in September 2022 while visiting Britain. Harry returned alone for his father’s coronation the following year and did not sit alongside other senior royals.
In February 2024, he traveled from the US to see Charles after he was diagnosed with cancer. More than a year later, they held another brief meeting in London.
Last month, Charles hosted Harry, Meghan and their children at Highgrove House. It was the monarch’s first meeting with Harry’s family in years and was viewed as a significant step toward repairing their relationship.
Harry has also returned to London several times since 2020 for charity events and court hearings related to his privacy case against Associated Newspapers.
According to media reports, the couple are due to move back to Britain later this month, with their children, Archie and Lilibet, expected to begin school in Britain in September.
Charles was reportedly informed of the decision last Sunday. There are no plans for either Harry or Meghan to resume duties as working royals.
Reports citing royal commentators said the family’s July visit was significant because the children were able to meet relatives they had rarely seen since the move to California.
According to the BBC, the decision was not driven by problems in the US but by the couple’s desire to spend more time in Europe, live closer to Harry’s family and educate their children in Britain.
Their precise destination has not been disclosed, although they are not expected to live in London. The Telegraph reported that they plan to settle in a “private, non-royal residence” near the capital.

China’s telecoms giants bet on ‘token factories’ as AI drives revenue growth
The country’s ‘big three’ telecoms operators are investing heavily in AI computing capacity, as they cash in on a surge in token usage
China’s three state-owned telecoms giants have made billable artificial intelligence tokens a key focus of their growth strategies, as AI adoption accelerates across the country and computing demand soars.
China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom all pointed to AI and computing operations as key growth drivers in their first-half financial disclosures released this month, presenting usage of tokens – the fundamental unit of data processed by AI models – as a central metric alongside others such as compute power and data.
On Thursday, China Telecom announced it had recorded a 95 per cent surge in intelligent computing revenue during the first half of the year. That drove a 7.1 per cent increase in its broader “intelligent business” revenue to 31.1 billion yuan (US$4.6 billion).
The company said it had also upgraded Xirang, its orchestration software for compute resources and networks, extending support to more than 20 chip architectures. Meanwhile, China Telecom Cloud revenue rose 7.8 per cent to 61.8 billion yuan.
China Unicom, which reported earnings on Tuesday, posted 41.9 billion yuan in computing-power revenue – a 13 per cent increase across data centres, leased compute, business software and cloud-based AI.
In its filing, Unicom pointed to its launch of a “token supermarket” – part of an end-to-end ecosystem to create, transfer, store and use AI tokens. Its UniAI platform connected more than 200 large language models and collected over 500 terabytes of high-quality data, it said.

China’s Own Version of Ambiguity in the Taiwan Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Taipei spent 10 days in August rehearsing a war with Beijing. Its annual Han Kuang exercise in 2026 simulated a blockade, attacks on critical infrastructure, disrupted internet, and the transition from peacetime to full-scale conflict. But this time, Beijing waited until the final day to issue its first official comment, dismissing the drills as a “wasteful charade.”
Beijing, in fact, appears to be cultivating a new form of “ambiguity” of its own. The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) remains active around Taiwan, but the balance of pressure has begun to look different. Compared with the dramatic encirclement exercises and large-scale military displays of recent years, Beijing’s military profile has been somewhat less conspicuous. Whether this reflects a deliberate signaling strategy cannot be established from open sources, but the broader pattern is obvious: in the first half of 2026, PLA fighter-jet activity around Taiwan fell to a three-year low.
That decline sits uneasily with the conventional assumption that Beijing is steadily escalating military preparations for reunification. It suggests, instead, that China may be shifting part of its pressure campaign away from highly visible military coercion toward methods that are less easily classified.
For example, while fighter jet numbers dropped, Taipei recorded 55 sightings of mainland Chinese government vessels around the island in June, including coast guard and research ships. That was 83 percent more than in May and 120 percent more than a year earlier. China has also begun coast guard patrols east of Taiwan, describing them not as military operations but as “routine law-enforcement patrols” in waters under Chinese jurisdiction.
In other words, Beijing is not necessarily reducing pressure; it is changing its form. Gray-zone activities blur the line between military coercion and civilian enforcement. This creates an emerging paradox in the Taiwan Strait. In Washington, an influential part of the policy community wants less ambiguity about what the United States would do if Beijing fights a war of reunification. Beijing, meanwhile, appears increasingly comfortable creating a new version of ambiguity.
Ambiguity Changes Hands
For decades, strategic ambiguity was primarily an American instrument. But the purpose was to restrain both sides, not simply to deter mainland China. Beijing was kept guessing about American intervention when fighting a war of reunification; Taipei was also left in the dark about how far American support would extend.
While Washington recognizes the People’s Republic of China as the sole legal government of China and maintains only unofficial relations with Taiwan, its “One China policy” remains distinct from Beijing’s “One China principle.” Washington acknowledges Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China without fully endorsing the PRC’s sovereignty claim over the island. At the same time, the United States does not support Taiwan independence.
This sort of ambiguity helped sustain a political middle ground in the Taiwan Strait and even the larger Asia-Pacific for a long time. Beijing could not assume that Washington would stand aside if it resorted to force, while Taipei could not assume that the United States would back a unilateral move toward formal independence. Crucially, neither side could be certain where Washington would stand if one day Beijing moved decisively toward unification, or Taipei toward formal independence. In a nutshell, this ambiguity was designed to preserve a status quo whose final political meaning in the Taiwan Strait remained deliberately unsettled.
Although supporters of strategic ambiguity still see value in its ability to restrain both Beijing and Taipei, calls for “strategic clarity” have grown louder in Washington, including among senior policymakers and national security officials. Advocates of strategic clarity argue that China’s military capabilities have expanded sharply and the consequences of miscalculation have become more severe.
Yet strategic clarity does not necessarily produce a clearer strategic environment in the Taiwan Strait. By weakening the old system of dual restraint, under which Beijing could not assume U.S. nonintervention and Taipei could not assume unconditional American support, it may instead encourage both sides to test the limits of the new arrangement. For Beijing in particular, clearer American red lines create stronger incentives to operate below them.
The result, then, is the relocation of the “ambiguity” argued above. As Washington seeks greater clarity in its commitments, Beijing is increasingly creating ambiguity through gray-zone activities that are harder to identify and even to answer with a proportionate response.
Different Understandings of the Status Quo
For decades, U.S. strategic ambiguity helped preserve a tacit understanding among Washington, Beijing, and Taipei about the status quo in the Taiwan Strait. The three sides never agreed on what the status quo ultimately meant, but ambiguity allowed them to live with that disagreement. Washington avoided endorsing either unification or formal independence. Beijing tolerated an unresolved political reality as long as the One China framework remained intact. Taipei, meanwhile, maintained its de facto autonomy without formally crossing the line toward independence.
This uneasy equilibrium depended less on a shared definition of the status quo than on a shared willingness not to force the question. As ambiguity begins to change hands, however, that tacit understanding is steadily breaking down.
Beijing is trying to define the status quo in the Taiwan Strait by its grey-zone activities. In May, China’s Foreign Ministry stated explicitly that “the two sides of the Strait belong to one China, and this is the ‘real’ status quo across the Taiwan Strait.” From Beijing’s perspective, it isn’t China that is gradually changing the status quo, but Taiwan’s leaders and “outside powers” – by hollowing out the One China framework.
This matters because the three sides interpret Beijing’s gray zone activities, its new form of ambiguity, in very different ways. Taipei sees coast guard patrols east of Taiwan, along with the growing presence of other civilian and government vessels, as incremental attempts to establish jurisdiction in areas where Beijing has not previously exercised it. Washington often views such activities as coercive actions below the threshold of war. Beijing, however, describes the same behavior as entirely “normal.” If Taiwan is part of China, then in Beijing’s legal and political logic, a Chinese coast guard vessel operating around the island is simply carrying out a domestic law enforcement function.
Four Audiences, Four Stories
Beijing’s new ambiguity is not aimed at Taipei and Washington alone. It can tell different stories to at least four audiences.
The first audience is the Chinese public. Beijing has long tied national rejuvenation to eventual unification, but repeated military threats create a credibility problem of their own. If every major exercise is presented as another step toward war, but that war never materializes, the signal can gradually lose its force. Yet actually launching a war would carry immense economic and political costs.
Thus gray zone actions offer Beijing a useful middle ground. They allow the leadership to argue that sovereignty is not merely a goal to be realized through some future campaign; it is already being exercised, incrementally and visibly. A coast guard patrol, in this sense, can demonstrate progress without forcing Beijing to make the far more consequential decision to go to war.
The second audience is Taipei. Overt military intimidation can easily backfire. Large-scale exercises and missile launches strengthen Taipei’s preferred narrative of democratic defense against an “authoritarian” power. High-profile military actions by China can reinforce Taiwanese support for higher defense spending, closer ties with Washington, and an increasingly distinct Taiwanese identity. Routine civilian activity works differently. A Chinese coast guard vessel appearing for the first time east of Taiwan may generate headlines, but after these vessels show up every month, or even every week, the media – and society – starts to lose interest. Beijing does not need Taiwanese society to accept its sovereignty claim. It may be enough to make certain activities seem less exceptional over time.
The third audience is Washington. Here, Beijing’s operational ambiguity runs directly into the American debate over strategic clarity. The United States can make clear that it can arm Taiwan, strengthen its regional posture, and prepare for the possibility of a blockade. But what should it do about a coast guard inspection or a fisheries-protection patrol? The clearer Washington becomes about the actions that could trigger military intervention, the stronger Beijing’s incentive to concentrate on those actions that do not.
This does not mean strategic clarity causes Chinese coercion. Beijing has its own objectives and has been increasing pressure on Taiwan for years. But greater U.S. clarity can change the tactics Beijing chooses to employ. Clear red lines work best when the prohibited act is easy to identify. They are far less effective against a strategy built from dozens of individually limited or ambiguous moves, none of which clearly crosses the threshold.
The fourth audience is the rest of Asia, especially the governments of Southeast Asia. For them, Beijing’s ambiguity creates a different kind of pressure about choosing sides. In August, while Taiwan’s Han Kuang exercise was underway, Chinese and Indonesian naval vessels conducted what Beijing called a navigation exercise east of Taiwan. Taipei condemned it as a dangerous attempt to strengthen China’s jurisdictional claims. Jakarta, however, described the encounter as a routine passing exercise unrelated to war fighting.
The contrast is also revealing for regional actors. A missile launch or military exercise is easy to recognize as a crisis, while a civilian exercise is much harder to classify. Many Southeast Asian governments therefore have strong incentives to treat such incidents as limited disputes and to avoid endorsing either Taipei’s or Beijing’s stance. This does not mean they necessarily accept China’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan. It means Beijing’s new type of ambiguity gives them political room to stay on the sidelines and for Beijing that is already a strategic gain. The less clearly an action looks like military coercion, the harder it becomes for Washington and Taipei to build a broad regional response around it.
Clarity Is Not a Guarantee
Against the pressure from Beijing, Washington’s strategic clarity seems a good offer for Taipei. The stronger the promise from Washington, the stronger the deterrent against Beijing seems to become. But it can easily go too far. The Taiwan Relations Act just requires the United States to maintain the capacity to resist force or coercion against Taiwan; it does not require Washington automatically to enter a war on Taiwan’s behalf. Even today, strategic clarity remains a proposal debated in Washington rather than a treaty-like security guarantee.
Nor should stronger American support be confused with support for whatever political course Taipei chooses. Washington’s One China policy has always combined assistance to Taiwan with restraints on Taiwan. The United States opposes unilateral changes to the status quo, but that applies to both sides of the Taiwan Strait. In that sense, repeated demands for ever clearer American signals can become counterproductive. Greater clarity may reassure Taiwan in the short term, but it can also weaken the uncertainty that once constrained political risk-taking by both Beijing and Taipei. If Taipei begins to treat “clearer” rhetorical support from Washington as evidence of an eventual U.S. commitment to fight under almost any circumstances, it risks confusing political sympathy with strategic obligation.
American interests in the Taiwan Strait are substantial, but they are not identical to Taiwan’s. No responsible U.S. government can write Taipei a blank check whose terms are determined by decisions made on the island.
Beijing watches this debate closely. From its perspective, increasingly explicit U.S. political and security signals to Taiwan can look less like deterrence and more like evidence that the old One China policy is being hollowed out. That perception helps explain why Beijing is turning to its own forms of ambiguity. The more clearly Washington signals where overt military action might trigger a response, the more incentive Beijing has to employ civilian ships in the strait that remain below that threshold. Strategic clarity, in other words, may deter one form of pressure while encouraging another.
Taipei has good reason to strengthen its defenses and deepen relations with Washington. But Taipei cannot guarantee Taiwan’s security by extracting ever more explicit promises from Washington. Taipei must also avoid political signals that can be interpreted in Beijing as an effort to use American backing to make the status of separation irreversible.
The lesson is that the clarity Taipei or Washington seeks has limits. Peace in the Taiwan Strait has historically depended not on unconditional guarantees, but on all three sides believing that restraint remains preferable to testing one another’s red lines. That restraint also matters to the wider region. For Japan and some Southeast Asian states, stability in the Taiwan Strait is less about choosing between competing political narratives than about preventing a crisis that would disrupt supply chains and regional security. If mutual restraint disappears, even the clearest American promise may produce a less predictable Taiwan Strait, and eventually leave the rest of Asia paying the price.

Australia and Thailand Deepen Ties to Hedge Against Global Uncertainty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:29:00 UTC
22:29:00 KST

In recent months, the Australia government has been incredibly active on the diplomatic front, from new security agreements with multiple Pacific Island countries to visits to Australia by the Japanese, Indian, New Zealand, and Vietnamese leaders. This week Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul made his way to Australia.
For both Canberra and Bangkok, there is a desire to build more substantive regional relationships as a hedge against both a more unreliable Washington and a more assertive Beijing – as well as buttress against the rippling effects of the competition between the two superpowers. The Australia-Thailand relationship is therefore less about alliance-building than about building greater resilience through diversifying partnerships, and creating a latticework of cooperation within the Indo-Pacific region.
The two prime ministers signed a series of agreements during Anutin’s visit that sought to give this strategy practical substance. These included deepening cooperation on transnational crime, including online scams, cybercrime, money laundering, human trafficking, and narcotics. The purpose of these agreements is to enable greater information sharing and coordination between the two countries’ law enforcement agencies.
Alongside this, the prime ministers committed to deepening economic engagement. Since the signing of the Thailand-Australia Free Trade Agreement in 2005, trade between the two countries has tripled, with Thailand becoming Australia’s fifth largest source of imports. But both countries believe there is room for expansion. They highlighted that cooperation across agriculture, clean energy, education, healthcare, critical technologies, resources, creative industries, and the digital economy were areas of greater ambition.
The other major announcement was the establishment of a biennial defense ministers’ meeting. The two countries have had a longstanding, but low-key, defense relationship. A bilateral military exercise called Thai Boomerang was established in 1992, and Thailand has participated in major multilateral exercises in Australia like Talisman Sabre. But consultation on defense policies has been limited. The establishment of a regular forum for the defense ministers to meet and coordinate is a positive elevation of the partnership.
It is unlikely that the two countries will become treaty allies anytime soon. Instead the deepening of the partnership is part of a strategy of diversifying partners, as well as an understanding of security in more holistic terms.
Anutin highlighted this in his August 18 address to the Lowy Institute in Sydney, titled “Beyond the Thailand-Australia Bilateral Strategic Partnership: Advancing International Order through Regional and Minilateral Cooperation.” In the speech, he argued that geopolitics, economics, and technology are becoming increasingly intertwined, leaving middle and smaller powers facing far more uncertainty. Rather than choosing sides in great power competition, Anutin argued that countries like Thailand and Australia have an interest in strengthening cooperation with each other and through regional institutions and smaller groupings.
There is also a recognition that the great powers are unavoidable. Thailand maintains strong ties with the United States, while also valuing its relationship with China. But when trust in a great power is low – as it is at present – other multilateral and minilateral institutions and cooperation gives middle and smaller powers greater options, more flexibility and room to maneuver.
This is particularly important as the concept of security becomes broader. Anutin described traditional defense cooperation alongside economic resilience, supply chains, technology, and energy as interrelated elements. He highlighted that this is increasingly a concern in Southeast Asia where there is a confluence of disrupted trade and energy flows, transnational crime, cyber threats, technological competition, and armed conflict. Australia stands as a trusted and low-friction partner able to help navigate this complexity.
For Australia, while the bilateral relationship is important, the more valuable element is further integration into the regional architecture. Australia’s ability to be seen as a trusted and important partner for ASEAN is vital for Canberra’s diplomatic priorities. The creation of the Office of Southeast Asia in 2022 within the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) was an indication of this priority. Alongside the Office of the Pacific, there is a level of senior coordination and bureaucratic focus that other regions are not afforded within Australian foreign policy.
This may seem odd given Australia’s security ties to the United States, its vast trading relationship with Northeast Asia, and its cultural links to Europe. But it’s a statement of where Canberra wants to be. The building of collaboration with countries like Thailand is central to Australia’s long-term strategic vision. This effort may be piecemeal and focused on practical cooperation, but it builds the relationship brick by brick, rather than through any single grand gesture.

US, Canadian trade teams meet again as tariffs deadline looms
WASHINGTON, Aug 21 - Top trade negotiators from Canada and the U.S. met for the third straight day in Washington on Friday to try to finalize a trade deal before threatened new U.S. tariffs were due to take effect on Saturday.
As talks continued on Friday afternoon, U.S. President Donald Trump said that he expected the two countries to reach an agreement, though he provided no details. He also said the United States was starting work towards a trade deal with Mexico.
"I have dealt with the prime minister, I have got a good relationship... The deal with Canada is moving along, and we should be able to have a deal with Canada," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, referring to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
A deal could mark a detente in what has been 18 months of tense relations that started when Trump imposed tariffs on key imports from Canada, prompting Ottawa to retaliate with a suite of countermeasures.
Trump says he will impose a new 50% tariff on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods at 12:01 a.m. EDT (0401 GMT) on Saturday if a deal is not reached.
Canada's minister responsible for trade with the U.S., Dominic LeBlanc, did not speak to reporters as he arrived for the talks.
LeBlanc met Greer for more than three hours on Thursday and said the two sides were "very close" to a deal, but added that more work was necessary.
Even if a deal is reached, Carney could find it hard to sell it to Canadians and the influential premiers of the 10 provinces.
A Leger opinion poll showed on Wednesday that 56% of Canadians want Carney to make no further concessions.
Sources say an agreement is expected to cut the tariff on Canadian-built vehicles to 15% from 25% and halve tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum to 25%. Ontario, a major steel and aluminum producer, wants the tariffs scrapped.
U.S. ALCOHOL
Carney is calling on major provinces to rescind their ban on sales of U.S. alcohol, which is a major irritant for Washington.
Wab Kinew, the premier of Manitoba, on Thursday said Trump was "very weak" and Canada should take advantage.
"I think we've got the upper hand - they're back on their heels right now. They're coming to us for a deal, and so I think we should fight," he told reporters.
Canada, though, is less than a tenth the size of the U.S. economy and sends around 70% of all exports south of the border, which makes it uniquely vulnerable to punitive U.S. trade actions.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday mocked Carney, saying he "comes in and puffs his chest out and says, 'I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump'."
In a recording obtained by the Canadian Press, Vance can then be heard saying "It's hilarious because Carney presents this as some victory for Canada when fundamentally, like, they climb down on a lot of issues."
Vance was speaking at a fundraiser in Southampton, New York. REUTERS

South African cyclist S’annara Grove provisionally suspended for failed doping test
LAUSANNE, Switzerland (AP) — South African cyclist S’annara Grove has been provisionally suspended because of a failed doping test, the International Testing Agency said Friday.
Grove’s sample collected on July 28 at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow returned an “adverse analytical finding” for ipamorelin, the ITA said.
Ipamorelin, prohibited in and out of competition, “is a synthetic peptide used to stimulate the body’s natural production of growth hormone,” the testing agency said.
The ITA said Grove, who didn’t medal in her track cycling events at the Commonwealth Games, has been informed of the case and has the right to challenge the provisional suspension.
The 32-year-old Grove rides professionally for the Smurfit Westrock team and is listed as a competitor in the current Tour of Britain. The third stage of the race was Friday.
Grove has not publicly addressed the ITA’s announcement. The Smurfit Westrock and South Africa teams have been approached for comment.
Grove had been scheduled to represent South Africa at the road world championships in Montreal in September.

Move over bears. Fat Marmot Week puts a spotlight on the alpine rodents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:23:01 UTC
22:23:01 KST

Move over bears. Fat Marmot Week puts a spotlight on the alpine rodents
Marmots have been studied in Gothic, Colorado since 1962, but that long-term research is in jeopardy amidst federal funding cuts. Researchers say their work studying the groundhog-like rodents is critical as global warming changes the alpine ecosystem they call home. (AP video by Brittany Peterson).
GOTHIC, Colo. (AP) — Last winter was tough for marmots living high in the Colorado mountains, where researchers say two-thirds of one population died while hibernating because of insufficient snow cover.
Those that survived are doing well, fattening up in time not just for fall and hibernation season but … drumroll, please … the very first Fat Marmot Week.
Just like Fat Bear Week, an online contest to vote for Alaskan brown bears plumped up for winter, Fat Marmot Week — beginning Monday — is mostly just for fun, but it also has a serious side: Scientists need to drum up donations for their long-running research into the rodents to keep it going through federal funding cuts.
“In some sense, we’re going to be laughing our way down as the Titanic sinks,” said Dan Blumstein, leader of the project launched decades ago at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Gothic, Colorado. “Because what else are you going to do?”
But wait. What’s a marmot?
A marmot is a cat-sized, furry ground squirrel that lives in burrows in North America, Europe and Asia. The 15 or so species worldwide include groundhogs, which have their own special day, Feb. 2, in the U.S. and Canada.
In the Rocky Mountains, yellow-bellied marmots are plentiful. Hikers often spot these charismatic creatures perched on boulders or scurrying through wildflowers.
Marmots aren’t shy near trails popular with people. Watch out: A bold one might swipe your snack.
Like people, marmots have personalities and are “flexibly social,” meaning some like to intermingle in colonies of up to 30 animals while others prefer solitude, according to Emily Renkey, a master’s program student at the University of California, Los Angeles.
“We kind of understand these marmots just by looking at them sometimes, because we can kind of tell who’s who just by how they behave and how they interact with one another,” said Katie Adler, a UCLA doctoral student.
Some marmots are difficult to study because they are wary of researchers’ efforts to trap them using wire boxes baited with an enticing mixture of oats and peanut butter, Renkey said.
“Others, you could trap three or four times in the same morning,” she said.
Marmots are big-time snoozers
While hibernating bears snooze in a state called torpor, allowing them to wake up — or be woken up — every now and then, marmots slip into a far deeper form of hibernation. Their body temperature drops from about that of a human to as low as 41 degrees Fahrenheit (5 degrees Celsius), not much warmer than their burrows in winter.
“You pick up a hibernating marmot and it’s this fuzzy ball and it feels like a cold rock with fur. It’s completely surreal,” Blumstein said. “They breathe once a minute or two.”
To prepare for winter, the animals do a tremendous amount of fattening. They double their weight to as much as 13 pounds (6 kilograms), then lose all of that bulk during half a year or more of hibernation.
“Marmots come out of the ground really skinny, relative to what they look like now, at least,” Adler said.
A poor snowpack affects more than the ski season
Last winter, scant snowfall and warm temperatures due to global warming deprived many Colorado marmots of an insulating blanket of snow over their burrows. Researchers believe their hibernation quarters got too chilly, causing many to die of cold.
“We had over 160 animals and we ended with 60 at the start of this season,” Blumstein said. “Most of them died because of the lack of snow cover.”
This year’s snowpack was the worst on record in the Upper Colorado River Basin, which includes Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico. Human-caused climate change made the snow drought about 14 times more likely, a new study confirms.
Hundreds of researchers at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory have observed changes including fewer bees and other pollinators, and sagebrush encroaching in valleys once dominated by wildflowers.
Precipitation changes, meanwhile, literally cascade downstream to where farmers and communities need water to survive.
“The snowmelt here impacts the Colorado River which impacts our drinking water,” Renkey said. “What happens in these mountains doesn’t stay in these mountains. It impacts all of us.”
Mouseketeers, musketeers and marmoteers
The study in Gothic, about 20 miles (32 kilometers) south of Aspen, is run by researchers from UCLA and the University of Ottawa in Ontario. It was launched in 1962, making it one of the world’s longest-running studies of individual mammals.
The marmot researchers affectionately call themselves “marmoteers.”
“It allows graduate students and other people to come in and suddenly capitalize on this knowledge and ask questions. Without doing all the grunt work,” Blumstein said.
Funding cuts have caused Blumstein’s UCLA department to lose one-third of its graduate students. Fat Marmot Week is one approach to attract interest — and hopefully donations — to keep the work going. Among the rodents on display: Stonehenge, who chirps at mountain bikers; and Citroen, whose mate is a leader of this matriarchal marmot motherland. Voting opens Monday.
The researchers have also been posting marmot videos to the OnlyFans adult content platform. To capitalize on the attention those posts have garnered, a “super fan” created a meme coin, a type of cryptocurrency, called $OnlyMarms, and donates transaction fees to the research program. That alone has raised around $100,000.
The team needs to bank three years of funding — over $200,000 — to ensure marmot research can continue next summer.
“People have to find funding in ways that we’ve never really thought of before,” Adler said. “Like reaching out to the broader community to get people engaged.”

Fears over conflicts, wildfires drive rise in cash holdings: European Central Bank economist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:20:24 UTC
22:20:24 KST

Burak Bir
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Europeans are holding on to more cash despite the rise of digital payments, with fears over wildfires, conflicts and other emergencies driving demand for banknotes, the chief economist of the European Central Bank (ECB) said Friday.
Despite contactless payments dominating in many European cities, the amount of cash in circulation is rising, ECB chief economist Philip Lane said at the MacGill summer school conference in Ireland.
"The total stock of banknotes is continuing to grow. In transactions, it [the number of notes] is coming down, but in terms of the stock [it is increasing]," Lane was quoted by British daily The Guardian as saying.
Last year, European citizens were advised to stockpile enough food, water and essentials for 72 hours in case of an emergency such as this summer’s catastrophic wildfires, floods or storms as well as potential cyber-attacks or other hostile events.
Also, households were encouraged to have a crisis pack including bottled water, a transistor radio, canned food and, critically, cash.
ECB data shows that the value of banknotes in circulation has gone up from about €1 trillion ($1.16T) in 2016 to €1.6 trillion ($1.87T) in June 2026.
Olive McCarthy, a professor at University College Cork said the continued use of cash was vital for people.
"While advice to maintain cash for emergencies is well made, and serves to remind us all to be prepared when digital systems let us down, it is essential that cash does not become viewed merely as a backup measure," she noted.
McCarthy added: "If we stop using it when there isn’t a crisis, it might not be easy to use it when there is."

From the Baltics to the U.S.: An E-2 Visa Roadmap for Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian Entrepreneurs  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:18:47 UTC
22:18:47 KST

Moving a business across borders requires careful planning. For entrepreneurs from Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania who want to enter the U.S. market, the E-2 treaty-investor visa can provide a practical route. Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, the classification is available to qualifying nationals of treaty countries who invest a substantial amount of capital in a real U.S. business and come to develop and direct it. The E-2 is a nonimmigrant classification, so it does not itself grant permanent residence. It can, however, support an extended U.S. business presence while the enterprise continues to meet the requirements.
Why the U.S. Market Appeals to Baltic Entrepreneurs
The United States offers a large customer base, investment networks, and opportunities to scale beyond the Baltic markets. These commercial advantages do not establish E-2 eligibility, but they can help show why the proposed U.S. enterprise is realistic.
Access to a Larger Customer Base
The U.S. population creates a market much larger than Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania combined. A business with proven demand may increase sales and build U.S. customer relationships. The E-2 application should support those expectations with credible market evidence.
Innovation Hub and Investor Capital
The United States is an important center for technology, research, and private investment. A U.S. presence may help Baltic businesses connect with customers, suppliers, partners, and investors. The business plan should explain how those relationships support the enterprise.
Diversification and Risk Mitigation
A U.S. operation may diversify revenue and reduce dependence on one regional market. The immigration case must still focus on the U.S. enterprise, committed investment, and the investor’s control.
How the E-2 Visa Supports International Business Expansion
The E-2 classification is designed for active investment, not passive ownership. State Department guidance in the Foreign Affairs Manual, section 402.9, requires a real and operating commercial enterprise, a substantial investment, an enterprise that is more than marginal, and an applicant who will develop and direct its operations.
Directing Your Investment
The investor must be in a position to develop and direct the enterprise. This usually requires control through at least 50 percent ownership, an equal partnership with enforceable management rights, or another arrangement that gives the investor genuine operational control. The rule does not require the investor to perform every daily task, but passive ownership is insufficient.
Bringing Key Personnel
A qualifying E-2 enterprise may also sponsor employees who share the enterprise’s treaty nationality. Under State Department guidance, the employee must generally serve in an executive or supervisory role or possess skills essential to the efficient operation of the business. Essential-skills cases depend on the employee’s qualifications, the business need, and the availability of those skills in the United States.
E-2 Eligibility for Citizens of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania
The State Department’s treaty-country list confirms that Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania qualify for E-2 visas. As of July 2026, the reciprocity schedules list multiple-entry E-2 visas with no reciprocity fee and maximum validity periods of 60 months for Estonian nationals, 34 months for Latvian nationals, and 12 months for Lithuanian nationals. Visa validity is different from the period of authorized stay granted at entry.
Nationality of the Investor
The principal applicant must be a national of a qualifying treaty country. If the enterprise is owned by an organization, nationals of the treaty country must own at least 50 percent of it for treaty-nationality purposes. A principal investor must also show personal control of the enterprise, normally through at least 50 percent ownership or another enforceable means of directing the business.
Intent to Depart
An E-2 applicant must intend to depart the United States when E-2 status ends. This is a legal eligibility requirement, not merely a formality. It does not prevent an applicant from later pursuing a lawful immigrant option, but the applicant must remain eligible for E-2 classification at the time of each application and admission.
Starting a New Company Versus Buying an Existing U.S. Business
An entrepreneur may establish a new company or acquire an existing U.S. business. Either route can qualify if the enterprise and investment meet the E-2 standards. The choice affects the evidence needed to establish cost, operations, financial viability, and control.
Advantages of Starting a New Business
Starting a business provides control over its products, systems, staffing, and culture. It may suit a company introducing a new service or extending an established Baltic operation into the United States. The investor must show that the enterprise will become real and operating rather than remain a paper organization or speculative investment.
Challenges of Starting a New Business
A new enterprise must establish operations, obtain required licenses, secure premises or systems, and develop customers. The application should document credible start-up costs, committed expenditures, operational steps, and a realistic path to revenue.
Advantages of Buying an Existing Business
Buying an operating business can provide customers, revenue history, employees, equipment, and established procedures. Those records may help demonstrate that the enterprise is real and operating, although the investment and control requirements still apply.
Challenges of Buying an Existing Business
Thorough due diligence is essential. The buyer should review financial records, taxes, contracts, licenses, liabilities, ownership, and employment matters. The transaction documents should also be coordinated with the immigration strategy so the funds are committed without exposing the buyer to avoidable closing risk.
What Makes an E-2 Investment Substantial?
There is no fixed minimum dollar amount for an E-2 investment. The State Department applies a proportionality test that compares qualifying funds invested with the cost of purchasing or establishing the business. Lower-cost businesses generally require a higher percentage of the total cost to be committed.
Proportionality to the Business Cost
For an existing business, cost is generally measured by the purchase price or fair market value. For a new enterprise, cost includes the expenditures needed to bring the business to the point of operation. The investment must also be large enough to show the investor’s financial commitment and support the likelihood of successful development and direction.
Investment Risk
The investor’s capital must be at risk in the commercial sense and subject to possible loss if the business fails. Funds held in a personal account or otherwise under the investor’s unrestricted control generally do not qualify. Loans secured only by the assets of the E-2 enterprise ordinarily do not establish the investor’s personal risk.
Proving That the Investment Funds Are Lawful and Committed
The investor must show lawful possession and control of the funds and document the path of the money into the U.S. enterprise. The Foreign Affairs Manual recognizes legitimate sources such as savings, gifts, inheritances, business or property sales, and loans secured by the investor’s personal assets.
Tracing the Funds
Evidence may include bank statements, tax records, payroll records, sale documents, gift records, loan documents, and transfer receipts. The records should connect the original source to each transfer and ultimately to the business expenditure or transaction.
Evidencing Commitment
Funds must be irrevocably committed to the enterprise. Payments for equipment, inventory, leases, professional services, or a business purchase may support that showing. A properly structured escrow arrangement can qualify when release is tied to visa approval, and the investor cannot freely withdraw the money for unrelated reasons.
Choosing a Business That Can Grow Beyond the Investor
The E-2 enterprise must be more than marginal. Under the Foreign Affairs Manual, a business is marginal if it lacks the present or future capacity to provide more than a minimal living for the investor and family, unless it has the capacity to make a significant economic contribution.
Job Creation Potential
There is no fixed number of U.S. jobs required. Hiring plans can nevertheless be persuasive evidence that the business will contribute beyond supporting the investor. Projections should identify realistic positions, timing, wages, and the business growth that will support those hires.
Not Just a Livelihood
A new business may rely on future capacity, but State Department guidance says that capacity should generally be achievable within five years after normal business activity begins. Revenue, profits, payroll, contracts, and expansion plans can all help establish that the enterprise is not marginal.
Building a Business Plan That Addresses E-2 Requirements
A detailed business plan can connect the investment evidence to the legal requirements, helping support successful E-2 visa filings, particularly for a new enterprise. It should be consistent with the supporting financial records and avoid unsupported assumptions.
Detailed Financial Projections
Five-year projections are commonly used for a new E-2 business because they address future viability and marginality. The forecasts should explain revenue, expenses, cash flow, profit or loss, and hiring assumptions. They should be tailored to the business and supported by credible market and cost data.
Operational Strategy and Market Analysis
The plan should explain the business model, customers, competitors, pricing, marketing, suppliers, and operating requirements. It should also show why the investor’s experience and control position support successful development of the enterprise.
Organizational Structure and Hiring Plans
The organizational chart should identify owners, managers, employees, and planned positions. Hiring projections should be realistic and consistent with the financial forecasts rather than included only to satisfy an assumed job-creation quota.
Preparing the Application and Consular Interview
Applicants outside the United States generally seek an E-2 visa through a U.S. embassy or consulate. An eligible person already in the United States may request a change or extension of E-2 status through USCIS, but approval of status does not issue a visa for later travel. Applicants should follow the current instructions of the relevant agency or consular post.
Assembling the Documentation
The filing should include proof of nationality, ownership and control, the lawful source and path of funds, committed investment, business operations, substantiality, and non-marginality. Required forms, document order, page limits, and submission methods may differ by consular post.
The Consular Interview
When an interview is required, the applicant should be prepared to explain the business, investment, source of funds, ownership, projected operations, and personal role. Answers should remain consistent with the application and supporting records.
Planning for Family, Renewals, and Long-Term U.S. Goals
A principal E-2 investor’s spouse and unmarried children under 21 may qualify for derivative E-2 status. The family should also distinguish temporary E-2 planning from any separate strategy for permanent residence.
Including Your Family
USCIS states that qualifying E spouses are generally employment-authorized incident to valid status when their documentation identifies them as an E spouse. They may apply for an Employment Authorization Document, but it is not always required before employment begins. E-2 children are not employment-authorized incident to status, although they may attend school.
E-2 Visa Renewals
Visa renewal at a U.S. consular post is different from extending E-2 status through USCIS. USCIS may grant qualifying investors and employees an initial stay of up to two years and extensions in increments of up to two years. Future applications require continued compliance with the E-2 rules, not automatic year-over-year growth.
Long-Term Immigration Strategies
E-2 classification does not directly convert to permanent residence. Some business owners may later qualify for another category, but each has separate requirements. For example, EB-1C generally requires a qualifying relationship between U.S. and foreign entities, at least one qualifying year of managerial or executive employment abroad, a managerial or executive U.S. role, and a U.S. petitioner that has been doing business for at least one year. Business growth or job creation alone is not enough.
Frequently Asked Questions
Are citizens of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania eligible for E-2 visas?
Yes. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are E-2 treaty countries. Applicants must also satisfy the other E-2 requirements, including making a substantial investment in a real U.S. business and having the ability to develop and direct that enterprise.
Is there a minimum investment amount for an E-2 visa?
No fixed minimum dollar amount applies. The investment is evaluated in proportion to the cost of purchasing or establishing the business. Lower-cost businesses generally require a higher percentage of the total business cost to be committed.
Can an E-2 investor buy an existing U.S. business?
Yes. An investor may either start a new company or acquire an existing U.S. business. A buyer should carefully review the business’s financial records, taxes, contracts, licences, liabilities, ownership, and employment matters before completing the transaction.
Does an E-2 business have to create U.S. jobs?
There is no fixed job-creation requirement. However, hiring plans can help show that the business is more than marginal and has the capacity to contribute economically beyond providing a minimal living for the investor and the investor’s family.
Can an E-2 visa lead directly to a green card?
No. E-2 classification does not directly convert to permanent residence. Some investors may later qualify for a separate immigrant category, such as EB-1C, but each category has its own eligibility requirements.

Pope says AI should be ‘servant of the common good,’ not humanity’s rival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-21
13:15:18 UTC
22:15:18 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
21 August 2026•Update: 21 August 2026
Pope Leo warned on Friday that AI must not be allowed to diminish humanity, urging political leaders to ensure technological innovation serves the common good.
Addressing members of the International Catholic Legislators Network, the pope said rapid development of artificial intelligence was raising one of the defining moral questions of the modern age.
“Every technological achievement also confronts humanity with a moral question: not merely what can we do, but what ought we to do?” he said.
Leo said lawmakers had a responsibility not to hinder innovation but to guide it wisely, calling for legislation that promotes scientific and technological progress while protecting fundamental rights and freedoms.
He said such policies should protect users from exploitation, preserve privacy, ensure transparency and strengthen democratic institutions.
The pope also warned that the rapid development of AI could create new forms of technological dependence, particularly for poorer countries, and risk becoming a tool of “ideological or economic colonialism.”
He pointed to concerns over algorithms determining “who is seen” or remains invisible, as well as digital platforms shaping public discourse without accountability.
“The world does not need an artificial intelligence that diminishes humanity,” Leo said.
“Only then will artificial intelligence become not a rival to humanity but a servant of the common good,” he added.

Somali child hunger crisis deepens as facilities close due to aid cuts, UNICEF says
Aug 21 - Nearly 1.9 million children in Somalia are expected to be malnourished this year, with the country seeing a 32% jump in the number of children admitted to facilities with severe acute malnutrition and complications, UNICEF said on Friday.
So far, 205 health and nutrition facilities have closed after unprecedented cuts to humanitarian aid, the United Nations children's agency said in comments delivered via video call by its spokesperson James Elder. As many as 618 health facilities could close nationwide, he said.
“Fewer facilities mean longer journeys for mums and their babies; longer journeys mean later treatment; later treatment means more severe illness and a greater risk of preventable death," Elder said.
“This is the wrong moment to retreat. Somalia is confronting a worsening climate crisis – severe drought in parts of the north, conflict and displacement, and, on the back of the war in Iran, rising costs for fuel and fertiliser."
Funding to tackle acute malnutrition in parts of Somalia has dropped by more than 80% this year, Médecins Sans Frontières said earlier in August, with the U.S. halting funds and other Western countries also cutting aid.
“This all sits side-by-side a terrifying reality in Somalia: this year nearly 1.9 million children are projected to be affected by malnutrition, including almost half a million with severe acute malnutrition, the deadliest form," Elder said. REUTERS

Production of 10m tons of greenhouse products targeted
TEHRAN- The Deputy Agriculture Minister for Horticulture Affairs announced the targeting of 10 million tons of production in the country's greenhouse sector and emphasized the necessity of moving from traditional methods toward advanced agriculture, along with removing infrastructural obstacles and active trade diplomacy for sustainable foreign currency generation.
According to an IRNA report, Mohammad Mehdi Boroumandi, on Wednesday at a specialized greenhouse growers' conference in Shiraz, while emphasizing the necessity of transitioning from traditional agriculture to advanced agriculture, announced the targeting of 10 million tons of production in the country's greenhouse development.
